title: A prayer as the seventh book begins
english: In the six books before this one, holy brother Ambrose, we have contended as well as we could against Celsus’s accusations against the Christians. So far as our strength allowed, we left nothing untested or unexamined and passed nothing by, but answered each point as best we could. Now we call upon God through Jesus Christ himself, the one whom Celsus accuses, that he, who is the Truth (John 14:6), may shine into our heart (2 Corinthians 4:6) what overturns falsehood; and so we begin this seventh treatise as well.

As we begin, we say to God in prayer that prophetic word: “In your truth destroy them” (Psalm 54:5). Plainly this means the arguments opposed “to the truth.” For these are destroyed by the truth of God, so that, once they are destroyed, everyone, set free from distraction, may say the words that follow: “Willingly I will sacrifice to you” (Psalm 54:6), and may offer to the God of the universe a rational sacrifice that sends up no smoke.

title: Celsus turns to the prophets
english: Celsus now sets out to attack the teaching which says that the things concerning Christ Jesus were foretold by the prophets among the Jews. And first, at the very start, we examine his view that those who bring in another god besides the God of the Jews can give no answer at all to his objections, while we, who have kept to the same God, take refuge in the defence drawn from the prophecies about Christ.

On this he says: “Let us see how they will find a way out. Those who bring in another god will find none; and those who keep the same God will once more say the same thing, that famous piece of wisdom, that it had to happen this way. And the proof? These things had been foretold long ago.”

To this we shall say that what he said a little earlier about Jesus and the Christians is so weak that even those who bring in another god, and do so impiously, could very easily answer what Celsus says. And if it were not improper to give the weaker an opening for accepting worse doctrines, we too would have done this, to prove false his claim that those who bring in another god have no defence against what Celsus has said. But as it is, come, let us make our defence about the prophets, in addition to what we have said above.

title: The Pythia and her unclean spirit
english: He says, then: “The things foretold by the Pythia, or by the priestesses of Dodona, or by the Clarian, or at Branchidae, or at the shrine of Ammon, and by countless other oracle-givers, under whose guidance nearly the whole earth was settled, these they count as nothing. But the things spoken, or not spoken, by those in Judaea after their fashion, the way people around Phoenicia and Palestine are still accustomed to do even now, these they think marvellous and unerring.”

Let us say, then, about the oracles he has listed, that we could collect from Aristotle and from those who have pursued philosophy in the Peripatetic school a good deal to overturn what is said about the Pythia and the other oracles. We could also set out what Epicurus and those who embrace his teaching have said on the same matters, and so show that some even among the Greeks overturn the oracles that are acknowledged and admired throughout all Greece.

But let it be granted that the accounts of the Pythia and the other oracles are not fictions, nor men’s pretence of being possessed by a god. Let us see, then, whether even so it cannot be proved to those who examine matters out of love for the truth that one who accepts these oracles as real need not admit that there are any gods in them, but, on the contrary, certain wicked demons and spirits hostile to the human race, which hinder the soul’s ascent, its journey by way of virtue, and its restoration to true piety toward God.

Now it is recorded of the Pythia, whose oracle seems more famous than the others, that Apollo’s prophetess, seated over the mouth of Castalia, receives a spirit through a woman’s private parts; filled with it, she utters the oracles that are held to be solemn and divine. See, then, whether this does not reveal how unclean and profane that spirit is. It enters the soul of the woman who prophesies, not through fine, unseen passages far purer than a woman’s private parts, but through those parts which a modest man may not rightly even look at, still less speak of or touch. And it does this not once or twice, which might perhaps have seemed more bearable, but as often as she is believed to prophesy from Apollo.

Moreover, to drive the supposed prophetess into ecstasy and a frenzied state, so that she is not aware of herself at all, is not the work of a divine spirit. For one who is held by the divine spirit ought to be benefited long before anyone at all who is taught by the oracles what helps toward ordinary, natural life, whether for profit or for advantage, and ought to see more clearly at that time above all when the divine is present with him.

title: Prophets enlightened, the Pythia darkened
english: Hence we, gathering our evidence from the sacred writings, show that the prophets among the Jews, enlightened by the divine Spirit as far as was useful to the prophets themselves as well, were the first to enjoy the coming of the higher power into them. Through the touch, if I may call it so, of what is called the Holy Spirit upon their soul, they became clearer-sighted in mind and brighter in soul, and in body too, since the body no longer worked against the life of virtue, being put to death as regards what we call “the mind of the flesh” (Romans 8:6). For we are persuaded that by a Spirit more divine “the deeds of the body” are put to death (Romans 8:13), deeds which take their rise from “the mind of the flesh,” the mind that is enmity toward God (Romans 8:7).

But if the Pythia is beside herself and not in her own mind when she gives oracles, what kind of spirit must we think it, which poured darkness over her mind and her reasoning, if not one of the same kind as the race of demons? Not a few Christians drive these out of those who suffer from them, without any occult or magical practice or use of drugs, but by prayer alone and very simple adjurations, and such things as the plainest person could use. For, as a rule, it is unlearned people who do this, since the grace that is in the word of Christ shows how worthless and weak the demons are: to be beaten, to give way, and to withdraw from a man’s soul and body, they by no means require someone wise and powerful in reasoned proofs of the faith.

title: Earthbound spirits behind the oracles
english: Moreover, it is believed not only among Christians and Jews but also by many others, both Greeks and barbarians, that the human soul lives and exists after its separation from the body. Reason, too, establishes that the pure soul, not weighed down by the lead weights of wickedness, is borne aloft to the regions of the purer, ethereal bodies, leaving behind the gross bodies here below and their defilements; while the wicked soul, dragged down to the earth by its sins and unable even to recover its breath, is carried about here and rolls around, one about “the tombs,” where “apparitions” of shadowy souls have even been seen (Plato, Phaedo 81c–d), another simply about the earth. If so, what sort of spirits must we think those are which have been bound, as it were, for whole ages (if I may put it so) to buildings and places, whether by certain spells or because of their own wickedness? Reason requires us to regard such beings as wicked: they use the power of foreknowledge, which is in itself neither good nor bad, to deceive men and to draw them away from God and from pure piety toward him.

That they are of this sort is shown also by this: their bodies are fed on the fumes that rise from sacrifices and on the vapours given off by blood and burnt offerings, in which they take delight, and so they come to this very thing, a kind of clinging to life, like wicked men who do not welcome the purer life apart from bodies, but for the sake of bodily pleasures cherish life in the earthy body.

If the Apollo at Delphi were a god, as the Greeks think, whom should he rather have chosen as his prophet than the wise man, or, if no such man was found, at least one who was making progress? And how could he not have wished a man, rather than a woman, to prophesy? And if he did want the female sex, perhaps because he could work through nothing else, or took pleasure in nothing else, than the private parts of women, how should he not rather have chosen a virgin than a woman to declare his will?

title: What Apollo’s choices reveal
english: But as it is, the Pythian god admired among the Greeks judged no wise man, and indeed no man at all, worthy of what the Greeks suppose to be divine possession. Nor, even among the female sex, did he choose a virgin, or a wise woman who had profited from philosophy, but some ordinary woman. Perhaps the better sort among human beings were too good for his work of possession.

Again, if he were a god, he ought to have used his foreknowledge as a bait, so to speak, for the conversion, the healing, and the moral reform of men. But as it is, history hands down nothing of the kind about him. For even if he said that Socrates was the wisest of all men, he blunted that praise by what he said about Euripides and Sophocles, in the line: “Sophocles is wise, Euripides wiser.” So Socrates was judged better than tragic poets whom the god had called wise, men who compete on the stage and in the orchestra for some trifling prize, and who sometimes stir grief and pity in the audience and sometimes unseemly laughter (for that is what satyr plays aim at). Ranked above such men, Socrates is hardly shown to have the dignity that comes from philosophy and truth, a dignity worthy of praise.

And perhaps he called him the wisest of all men not so much for his philosophy as for the sacrifices and the smoke of burnt fat that he offered to him and to the other demons. And it is for these things, it seems, rather than for works of virtue, that the demons do what is asked by those who bring them offerings. That is why Homer, the best of the poets, describing what happens and teaching what chiefly persuades the demons to do what those who sacrifice want, brought in Chryses: for the sake of a few garlands and the thighs of bulls and goats, he obtained what he asked against the Greeks on account of his daughter, that they should be struck with plague and give Chryseis back to him (Homer, Iliad 1.37–42). I remember reading in one of the Pythagoreans, who wrote about what the poet said in a hidden sense, that Chryses’ words to Apollo, and the plague sent by Apollo upon the Greeks, teach that Homer knew that certain evil demons, who delight in the smoke of fat and in sacrifices, pay those who sacrifice with the ruin of others, if that is what the sacrificers pray for.

And “the lord of wintry Dodona,” at whose shrine are the prophets “with unwashed feet, who sleep on the ground” (Homer, Iliad 16.234–235), rejected the male sex for prophecy and uses the women of Dodona, as Celsus too has pointed out. Granted that there is someone much like these at Claros, another at Branchidae, another at Ammon’s shrine, or wherever on earth they give oracles: how then will it be shown that they are gods, and not some demons?

title: Prophets whose lives were worthy of the Spirit
english: Among the prophets of the Jews, some were wise before they received prophecy and divine possession; others became wise when their minds were enlightened by the prophecy itself. They were chosen by providence to be entrusted with the divine Spirit and the words that come from him because of their way of life: a life hard to imitate, exceedingly strenuous and free, and wholly undaunted in the face of death and danger. For reason, too, shows that the prophets of the God who is over all must be such men. They made the hardihood of Antisthenes, Crates and Diogenes look like a game. At any rate, for the sake of truth and for rebuking sinners freely, “they were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were tempted, they died by the sword; for they went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, ill-treated, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth, men of whom the world on earth was not worthy” (Hebrews 11:37–38). They always fixed their gaze on God and on the invisible things of God, which are not seen by the senses and are for that reason eternal (2 Corinthians 4:18).

The life of each of the prophets has been recorded. For the present it is enough to set before you the life of Moses (for prophecies of his, too, are handed down, written in the law); that of Jeremiah, related in the prophecy that bears his name; and that of Isaiah, who, going beyond every discipline, walked “naked and barefoot” for three years (Isaiah 20:2–3). Look also at the robust life of the boys, Daniel and his companions, when you have read that they drank water and that their food was pulse, since they abstained from living things (Daniel 1:12–16). And if you can, consider also what came before them: Noah, who prophesied (Genesis 9:25–27); Isaac, who prayed prophetically over his son (Genesis 27:27–29); and Jacob, who said to each of the twelve, “Come, that I may tell you what will happen in the last days” (Genesis 49:1). These men, and countless others who prophesied for God, also foretold what concerns Jesus the Christ.

That is why we hold in no account the things foretold by the Pythia, or the priestesses of Dodona, or the Clarian, or at Branchidae, or at the shrine of Ammon, or by countless other so-called oracle-givers. But what was prophesied by those in Judaea fills us with awe, for we see that their robust, strenuous and dignified life was worthy of the Spirit of God, who prophesies in a new way, nothing like the divinations that come from demons.

title: The Spirit has left the Jews, but traces remain
english: I do not know why Celsus, after saying “the things spoken by those in Judaea after their fashion,” added “or not spoken,” claiming, as an unbeliever would, that these things may never have been spoken at all, and that perhaps things never spoken were written down. For he did not look at the dates, nor the fact that many years beforehand the prophets foretold countless things and spoke also of the coming of Christ.

Again, wishing to slander the ancient prophets, he says that they prophesied in the way “that those around Phoenicia and Palestine,” he says, “are still accustomed to do even now.” He does not make clear whether he means people who are strangers to the teaching of the Jews and Christians, or people who prophesy in the Jewish way, after the pattern of the prophets. But however his words are taken, they are shown to be false. For neither have any of those outside the faith done anything like what the prophets did, nor is anyone recorded as having prophesied among the Jews in later times, after the coming of Jesus. For it is acknowledged that the Holy Spirit has left them, because they acted impiously toward God and toward the one whom their own prophets foretold.

Signs of the Holy Spirit were shown at the beginning of Jesus’ teaching, and more after his ascension, but fewer later. Yet even now traces of the Spirit remain among a few, whose souls have been cleansed by the Word and by actions done in keeping with the Word. “For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee from deceit, and will rise and depart from senseless thoughts” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:5).

title: Celsus describes the prophets of Phoenicia and Palestine
english: Since Celsus also promises to describe the manner of the oracles in Phoenicia and Palestine, as one who has heard them and learned all about them, come, let us look at this too. First he says that there are several kinds of prophecy, but he does not set them out; for he had none to set out, and was only making a false show. But let us see what he says is the most perfect kind among the men of that region.

“Many nameless men,” he says, “very readily and on any chance occasion, both in temples and outside temples, and others who go begging and roam about cities or army camps, are stirred, so they make out, as though uttering oracles. Each has ready on his lips the customary words: ‘I am God, or a son of God, or a divine spirit. And I have come; for already the world is perishing, and you, O men, are going to ruin because of your wrongdoing. But I wish to save you. And you will see me coming back again with heavenly power. Blessed is he who worships me now; but on all the rest I will cast eternal fire, on cities and on lands alike. And men who do not know the punishments in store for them will repent in vain and groan; but those who have been persuaded by me I will keep for ever.’”

Then next he says: “Having brandished all this, they go on to add unintelligible, frenzied and altogether obscure words, whose meaning no one with any sense could discover; for they are unclear and mean nothing, but they give any fool or sorcerer an opening to seize on what was said and make it his own, on any matter and in whatever way he wishes.”

title: Why the prophets spoke in riddles
english: But if he had been fair in his accusation, he ought to have set out the prophecies word for word, whether those in which the speaker announced himself to be God almighty, or those in which he announced himself the Son of God, or those in which the speaker was believed to be the Holy Spirit. For then he would have been making a real effort to overturn what was said and to show that the words were not inspired, words that contain a call to turn from sins, a rebuke of the people of that day, and foreknowledge of things to come. That is why those who lived in the prophets’ own time wrote down their prophecies and preserved them: so that later generations too, reading them, might marvel at them as words of God; and, helped not only by the rebukes and calls to conversion but also by the predictions, and convinced by the outcome of events that it was a divine Spirit who had foretold them, might persevere in practising the piety that accords with the word, obeying the law and the prophets.

The prophets, then, in accordance with the will of God, spoke without any concealment whatever their hearers could usefully understand at once and whatever helped to correct their conduct. But what was more mystical, more for the eyes of the initiated, and bound up with a contemplation beyond what the common ear can take in, they set forth “through riddles” (Numbers 12:8), through allegories, through what are called dark sayings, and through what are named parables or proverbs (Proverbs 1:6). They did this so that those who do not shrink from toil, but take on every labour for the sake of virtue and truth, might examine and find, and, having found, might put what they found to use as reason requires.

But the noble Celsus, as though angry at not having understood such words of the prophets, reviled them, saying: “Having brandished all this, they go on to add unintelligible, frenzied and altogether obscure words, whose meaning no one with any sense could discover; for they are unclear and mean nothing, but they give any fool or sorcerer an opening to seize on what was said and make it his own, on any matter and in whatever way he wishes.” He seems to me to have said this with cunning, wishing, so far as lay in his power, to keep readers of the prophecies from testing and examining their meaning. And something has happened to him like what happened to those who said of a certain prophet, who had gone in to someone and foretold the future to him: “Why did this madman come in to you?” (2 Kings 9:11).

title: Obscure, but not meaningless
english: It is likely, then, that there are arguments far wiser than our ability allows, which could show that Celsus is lying here and that the prophecies are inspired. Still, we too have done what we could: in the works we have composed on Isaiah, on Ezekiel and on some of the Twelve, we have explained word by word the passages that Celsus calls “frenzied and altogether obscure.” And if God grants progress in his word, at the times he wills, there will be added to what we have already dictated on these books either what is still lacking or as much as we manage to make clear.

Others too, who wish to examine Scripture and have sense, would be able to find its meaning. It is truly unclear in many places, but it is not, as Celsus says, “nothing.” Nor can any fool or sorcerer smooth it out, or make what was said his own in whatever way he likes. Only the one who is truly wise in Christ, and every such person, could set out the whole connected sense of what was spoken with concealment in the prophets, “comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (1 Corinthians 2:13) and establishing each thing he finds from the usage of the Scriptures.

We must not believe Celsus when he says that he heard such men with his own ears. For in Celsus’s time there were no prophets like those of old; otherwise their prophecies too would have been written down one after another by those who accepted and admired them, as were the writings of long ago. And Celsus’s lie seems to me wholly plain from his claim that these supposed prophets whom he heard in person, when Celsus refuted them, admitted to him what they were after, and that they had been making it up, saying things that meant now one thing, now another. He ought also to have given the names of those he claimed to have heard in person, so that from the names, if he had any to give, it might be clear to those able to judge whether he was telling the truth or lying.

title: Celsus names no shameful passage
english: He also thinks that those who use the prophets to defend what concerns Christ can say nothing to the point whenever something wicked, shameful, unclean or foul appears to be said about the Deity. So, as though no defence existed, he strings together countless arguments for himself on points that are not granted.

But it must be understood that those who wish to live by the divine Scriptures, who know that “the knowledge of the senseless is unexamined words” (Sirach 21:18), and who have read the words “always ready to make a defence to everyone who asks us for an account of the hope that is in us” (1 Peter 3:15), do not take refuge only in the fact that these things were foretold. They also try to resolve the apparent incongruities, and to show that there is nothing wicked, shameful, unclean or foul in the words, but that they become so for those who do not understand the divine Scripture as it ought to be interpreted.

He ought to have set out from the prophets what appears wicked in them, or what seemed shameful to him, or what he thought unclean, or what he took to be foul, if he really saw such things said in the prophets; for his argument would then have struck harder and done more to achieve what he wanted. As it is, he set nothing out, but with a threatening flourish he declares that such things appear in the Scriptures, and in this he lies about them. No reason, then, requires a defence against mere empty noises of words, to show that there is nothing wicked, shameful, unclean or foul in the words of the prophets.

title: What Christ suffered was not defilement
english: But God neither does nor suffers the most shameful things, nor does he serve evil, as Celsus supposes; for nothing of the kind was foretold. And if he himself says that it was foretold that God would serve evil, or do or suffer the most shameful things, he ought to have quoted the prophets’ words to that effect, instead of wishing to defile his hearers to no purpose.

What Christ would suffer, the prophets did foretell, and they also set down the reason why he would suffer; and God knew what his Christ would suffer. But on what grounds were these things most foul and most unclean, as Celsus says? He will seem, though, to be showing how the things Christ endured were most foul and most unclean, since he says: “For what else was it for God to eat the flesh of sheep and to drink gall or vinegar, but to eat dung?”

But God, on our teaching, did not eat the flesh of sheep. For even supposing he did eat, it was as one who bore a body that Jesus ate. As for the gall and the vinegar, which were prophesied in the words, “They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 69:21), we have spoken of them earlier, and Celsus forces us to say it again. For those who plot against the word of truth always bring to the Christ of God the gall that comes from their own wickedness and the vinegar that comes from their own turning toward what is base; and he, “when he has tasted it, will not drink” (Matthew 27:34).

title: Celsus sidesteps the argument from prophecy
english: Then, after this, wishing to overthrow the faith of those who have accepted what concerns Jesus because it had been prophesied, he says: “Come now: if the prophets foretold that the great God (to say nothing more offensive) would be a slave, or fall sick, or die, will it then be necessary for God to die, or be a slave, or fall sick, since it had been foretold, so that by dying he might be believed to be God? But the prophets would not foretell this, for it is evil and unholy. So we must not consider whether they foretold it or did not foretell it, but whether the deed is worthy of God and good. What is shameful and evil we must disbelieve, even if all men, gone mad, should seem to foretell it. How then can the things done in his case, as though he were God, be holy?”

Through these words he appears to have suspected that the point about Jesus’ having been prophesied was a strong one for persuading those who hear it, and to be trying to overturn the argument with another plausible point, saying: “So we must not consider whether they foretold it or did not foretell it.” But if he wished to object to the claim by demonstration and not by fallacy, he ought to have said: “So we must show that they did not foretell it, or that the things said about Christ were not fulfilled in Jesus as they foretold,” and then to have added what seemed to him a demonstration.

In that way it would have become clear what the prophecies say that we apply to Jesus, and how he proves our interpretation false; and it would have been found out whether he nobly overturns what we bring from the prophets in support of our account of Jesus, or whether he is caught shamelessly trying to force the clear evidence of the truth to pass for something that is not true.

title: A Stoic proof turned against Celsus
english: He sets down, by way of hypothesis, certain things that are impossible for God and unfitting for him, and says: “If these things were prophesied of the God over all, must we, because they are foretold, believe such things of God?” He thinks he is establishing that, even if the prophets had truly foretold such things of the Son of God, it was impossible that one should have to believe the predictions that he suffered or did them. To this we must say that his hypothesis, being absurd, would produce conditionals that end in statements that contradict each other. This is shown as follows.

If the true prophets of the God over all should say that God would be a slave, or always be sick, or die, these things will happen to God, for the prophets of the great God must speak without falsehood. But also, if the true prophets of the God over all say these same things, then, since what is impossible by nature is not true, what the prophets say would not happen to God. Now when two conditionals end in statements that contradict each other, by the theorem called the argument from two conditionals, the antecedent common to both conditionals is refuted. Here that antecedent is that the prophets foretell that the great God will be a slave, or fall sick, or die. The conclusion is therefore: the prophets did not, then, foretell that the great God would be a slave, or fall sick, or die. And the argument falls under a mode of this kind: if the first, then the second; if the first, then not the second; therefore not the first.

The Stoics also apply this mode to a concrete case, saying: if you know that you are dead, you are dead; if you know that you are dead, you are not dead; and it follows: therefore you do not know that you are dead. They establish the conditionals in this way. If you know that you are dead, what you know is so; therefore it is so that you are dead. And again: if you know that you are not dead, and what you know is so, you are not dead; and since a dead man knows nothing, it is plain that if you know that you are dead, you are not dead. And from both conditionals there follows, as I said before: therefore you do not know that you are dead. Something like this holds also for Celsus’s hypothesis, in the words of his that we set out above.

title: The prophets foretold the death of a man
english: But not even the things we took up by way of hypothesis are like the prophecies about Jesus. For the prophecies did not foretell that God would be crucified. Of him who took death upon himself they say: “And we saw him, and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honour, falling short of the sons of men; a man stricken and in pain, and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:2–3). See, then, how plainly they have called a man the one who suffered human things. And Jesus himself, knowing exactly that what was dying was a man, says to those plotting against him: “But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from God” (John 8:40).

But if there was something divine in the man understood in him, namely the Only-begotten of God and “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), who says “I am the truth” (John 14:6), and “I am the life” (John 11:25), and “I am the door” (John 10:9), and “I am the way” (John 14:6), and “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51), then surely the account of him and of his essence is a different one from the account of the man understood in Jesus.

That is why not even the very simplest Christians, who have not been trained in critical reasoning, would say that the truth died, or the life, or the way, or the living bread that came down from heaven, or the resurrection. For he who, in the man seen in Jesus, taught the words “I am the resurrection” (John 11:25) says that he himself is the resurrection. Indeed, none of us is so witless as to say: “The life has died,” or “The resurrection has died.” Celsus’s hypothesis would have had some ground if we claimed that the prophets had foretold that God the Word would die, or the truth, or the life, or the resurrection, or any other of the things which the Son of God says he is.

title: What the prophets foretold was worthy of God
english: In this passage, then, Celsus speaks the truth on one point only: “But the prophets would not foretell this, for it is evil and unholy.” And what is “this” but that the great God will be a slave or will die? What the prophets prophesied is worthy of God: that a certain “radiance” and “imprint” (Hebrews 1:3) of the divine nature would come to dwell in this life together with the holy soul of Jesus as it became man, in order to sow a word that makes kin to the God of the universe the one who receives it into his own soul, tends it, and brings it all to completion. That word holds in itself the power of God the Word, who was to be in a human body and soul. Yet it will be in such a way that his rays are not shut up in him alone, and it is not said that the light which gives these rays, being God the Word, is nowhere else.

The things concerning Jesus, then, in so far as they are understood to have been done by the Godhead in him, are holy and do not conflict with the notion of the divine. But in so far as he was a man, adorned more than any other man by the highest share in the very Word and the very Wisdom, he endured, as one wise and perfect, what had to be endured by one who does all things on behalf of the whole human race, or even of rational beings.

And there is nothing absurd in the man’s having died, and in his death not only standing as an example of dying for the sake of godliness, but also having brought about the beginning and the advance of the destruction of the evil one, the devil, who had held the whole earth as his domain. The signs of his overthrow are those who, through the coming of Jesus, have everywhere escaped the demons that held them, and who, having been freed from slavery under them, devote themselves to God and to a godliness toward him that grows purer day by day, as far as they are able.

title: Celsus sets Moses against Jesus
english: Next after this Celsus says something like the following: “Will they not consider this point again? If the prophets of the God of the Jews foretold that this man would be his Son, how is it that through Moses he lays down that they are to be rich and hold power and fill the earth and slaughter their enemies young and old and kill them along with their whole race, which he himself also does before the eyes of the Jews, as Moses says, and besides this threatens outright, if they do not obey, to treat them as he treats their enemies (Numbers 33:56); while his Son, then, the Nazarene man, lays down contrary laws: that the man who is rich or loves power or lays claim to wisdom or glory has no access to the Father (Matthew 19:24), that one must take no more thought for food and storehouse than ‘the ravens’ do (Luke 12:24), and less for clothing than ‘the lilies’ (Luke 12:27), and that to one who has struck once one must offer oneself to be struck again (Luke 6:29)? Which of them is lying, Moses or Jesus? Or did the Father, when he sent this man, forget what commands he had given to Moses? Or did he condemn his own laws and change his mind, and is he now sending his messenger with the opposite charge?”

In saying this, Celsus, who professes to know everything, has made the mistake of a complete layman. As to the meaning of the Scriptures, he has supposed that the law and the prophets hold no deeper sense beyond the words taken by the letter. He does not see that Scripture would not have promised bodily wealth to those who lived rightly in a way so plainly unconvincing, when the most righteous men are shown to have lived in extreme poverty. The prophets, at any rate, who received the divine Spirit because they lived purely, “went about in sheepskins and goatskins, in want, afflicted, ill-treated, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth” (Hebrews 11:37–38); for “many are the afflictions of the righteous” (Psalm 34:19), as the psalmist says.

If Celsus did read the law of Moses, he probably supposed that the words “You shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow” (Deuteronomy 15:6), spoken to the one who keeps the law, meant this: that the righteous man is told, by way of promise, that he will grow so rich in blind wealth that, because of the abundance of his money, he will lend not only to Jews, and not just to one other nation, or a second, or a third, but to many. How much money, then, would the righteous man have possessed, having received it as the wage of his righteousness according to the law, so that he could lend “to many nations”? It follows from such an interpretation that one must also suppose that the righteous man never borrows, since it is written: “But you shall not borrow.”

Did the nation, then, remain for so long a time in the worship of God according to Moses, while it plainly saw, so far as Celsus’s view goes, that the lawgiver was lying? For no one is recorded to have grown so rich that he lent “to many nations”. But it is not plausible that they would have fought for the law if they had been taught to understand it as Celsus thought, and plainly saw that the law’s promises were false. And if someone brings forward the recorded sins of the people as proof that they despised the law, perhaps because they had condemned it as lying, we must tell him that he should also read of the times in which the whole people is recorded, after doing evil before the Lord (Judges 2:11), to have turned to the better and to the worship of God according to the law.

title: Promises that cannot be taken literally
english: Moreover, if the law promised them dominion when it said, “You shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you” (Deuteronomy 15:6), and nothing deeper is meant by these words, it is clear that the people would have condemned the promises of the law all the more. Celsus paraphrases certain words which suggest that the whole earth will be filled by the Hebrew seed. As a matter of history, this has come about after the coming of Jesus, because God was angry, if I may use that word, rather than because he was granting a blessing.

As for its being said to the Jews, by way of promise, that they would slaughter their enemies, we must say that anyone who reads and attends carefully to the words would find the literal interpretation impossible. For the present it is enough to cite from the Psalms the way in which the righteous man is introduced as saying, among other things, this too: “In the mornings I killed all the sinners of the earth, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work lawlessness” (Psalm 101:8).

Consider, then, the wording and the frame of mind of the speaker. After first telling of virtuous deeds, which lie open to anyone who wishes to read them, could he go on to state, as something literally possible, that at no other time of day than the early morning he slew “all the sinners of the earth”, so as to leave none of them alive? And did he really destroy from Jerusalem every single man who worked “lawlessness”? And you would find many such sayings in the law as well, such as “We did not leave any of them alive” (Deuteronomy 2:34).

title: The law in letter and in meaning
english: Celsus also cites the warning given them beforehand, that if they did not obey the law they would suffer the same things they were doing to their enemies. Before Celsus sets beside these passages, and puts to use, what he thinks are contradictions of the law drawn from the teaching of Christ, we must speak about what has been said so far.

We say, then, that the law is twofold: one law according to the letter, the other according to the meaning, as some of those before us have also taught. The law according to the letter is said to be “statutes not good” and “commandments not good” (Ezekiel 20:25), not so much by us as by God, who speaks in one of the prophets; but the law according to the meaning is said by the same prophet, speaking in the person of God, to be “good statutes” and “good commandments” (Ezekiel 20:11). For the prophet does not openly contradict himself in the same place. In keeping with this, Paul too said that “the letter” kills, which is the same as the law according to the letter, but “the spirit” gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6), which is equivalent to the law according to the meaning.

Indeed, one can find in Paul something that answers to what might be thought contradictions in the prophet. In one place Ezekiel says, “I gave them statutes that were not good and commandments that were not good, by which they shall not live” (Ezekiel 20:25), and in another, “I gave them good statutes and good commandments, by which they shall live” (Ezekiel 20:11), or at any rate words equivalent to these. So too Paul, where he wishes to disparage what belongs to the letter of the law, says: “If the ministry of death, carved in letters on stones, came in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze at the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, a glory that was passing away, how much more will the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?” (2 Corinthians 3:7–8). But where he admires and approves the law, he calls it spiritual, saying, “We know that the law is spiritual” (Romans 7:14); and he approves it in the words, “So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12).

title: The wealth that sees
english: If, then, the wording of the law promises wealth to the righteous, let Celsus, following the “letter” that kills (2 Corinthians 3:6), suppose that the promise speaks of blind wealth; but we take it to mean the wealth that sees sharply (Plato, Laws 631c): the wealth by which a man is rich “in all speech and all knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1:5), and the wealth meant when we charge “those who are rich in this present age not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides all things for enjoyment; to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous, ready to share” (1 Timothy 6:17–18). For “the wealth” that consists in true goods “is the ransom of a man’s soul”, according to Solomon, while the poverty opposed to it is ruinous; because of it “the poor man does not stand up to a threat” (Proverbs 13:8).

We must speak about dominion in the same way as we have spoken about wealth: the dominion by which “one” righteous man is said to pursue “a thousand, and two” to put “tens of thousands” to flight (Deuteronomy 32:30). If this is how the passages about wealth are understood, see whether it is not in keeping with God’s promise that the man who is rich “in all speech and all knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1:5), and in all wisdom, and in every good work, lends “to many nations” (Deuteronomy 15:6) out of his wealth in the word and in wisdom and knowledge, just as Paul lent when, “from Jerusalem and round about” as far as “Illyricum”, he fully preached “the gospel of Christ” (Romans 15:19) to all the nations he visited. And since divine things were made known to him by revelation (Ephesians 3:3), his soul being enlightened by the divinity of the Word, for this reason he himself did not borrow, nor did he need any man to minister the word to him.

And since it is also written in the same way, “You shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you” (Deuteronomy 15:6), Paul, by the dominion that comes from the word, brought those from the nations under the teaching of Christ Jesus and ruled over them, never standing in the place of one subject to men as though they were his betters. In this way, too, he filled the earth.

title: Slaying the infants of Babylon
english: And if we must also explain the slaughtering, and with it the righteous man’s power in all things, we must say that when he says, “In the mornings I killed all the sinners of the earth, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work lawlessness” (Psalm 101:8), by “earth” he meant figuratively the flesh, whose “mind” “is enmity against God” (Romans 8:7), and by the city “of the Lord” his own soul, in which there was “a temple of God” (1 Corinthians 3:16), since he had received a right opinion and conception of God, one admired by all who saw it.

So at the moment when the rays of the sun “of righteousness” (Malachi 4:2) shone upon his soul, as though empowered and strengthened by them, he slew every “mind of the flesh” (Romans 8:7), which is called “sinners of the earth”, and destroyed from “the city of the Lord” within his own soul all the thoughts “that work lawlessness” and the notions hostile to the truth. In this way too the righteous destroy every living remnant (Deuteronomy 2:34) of the enemies, the ones that come from wickedness, so that not even an infant evil, just beginning to sprout, is left.

So too we understand the text in the hundred and thirty-sixth psalm, which runs thus: “O wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you the recompense with which you repaid us; blessed is he who will seize your infants and dash them against the rock” (Psalm 137:8–9). For the “infants of Babylon”, a name that is interpreted “confusion”, are the confusing thoughts arising from wickedness that have just sprung up and are rising in the soul. The man who seizes them, so as to break their heads against the firmness and strength of the word, dashes “the infants” of “Babylon” “against the rock”, and for this reason becomes “blessed”.

Let God, then, command that the things of wickedness be slain “young and old” and “along with their whole race”; in this he teaches nothing contrary to what Jesus proclaimed. And let God bring about, “before the eyes” of those who are Jews “in secret” (Romans 2:29), the destruction of the enemies and of all that comes from wickedness. And let this be what is meant by saying that those who do not obey the law and word of God, having become like the enemies and been shaped by wickedness, shall suffer these things, which those who have fallen away from the words of God deserve to suffer.

title: Wealth, rule and wisdom in the teaching of Jesus
english: From these points too, then, it is clear how Jesus, the “Nazarene” man, does not lay down contrary laws in what he said about wealth and about those who were amazed, namely, that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God (Mark 10:23–26; Luke 18:24). This holds whether one takes the “rich man” more simply as the one who is distracted by wealth and hindered by it, as by thorns, from bearing the fruits of the word (Matthew 13:22), or as the one who is rich in false doctrines, of whom it is written in Proverbs: “Better a poor man who is righteous than a rich man who is a liar” (Proverbs 19:22).

It is likely that Celsus took the idea that Jesus forbade the love of rule from the sayings “Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be the servant of all” (Mark 10:43–44; compare Mark 9:35), “The rulers of the nations lord it over them” (Matthew 20:25), and “Those who exercise authority among them are called benefactors” (Luke 22:25). This must not be thought contrary to “You shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you” (Deuteronomy 15:6), especially in view of the explanations already given of that text.

Next after these points Celsus throws in something about wisdom, supposing that Jesus teaches that the wise man has no access to the Father. Let us say to him: Which wise man? If he means the one who has been shaped by what is called the wisdom “of this world,” which is foolishness “with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19), we too shall say that the man who is wise in this way has no access to the Father. But if one understands Wisdom to be Christ, since Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), we say not only that the man who is wise in this way has access to the Father; we also say that the one adorned with the gift called the word of “wisdom,” which is given through the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:8), far surpasses those who are not such.

title: Glory, food and clothing in the law and the Gospel
english: Again, we say that laying claim to glory from men is forbidden not by the teaching of Jesus alone but also by the old Scripture. One of the prophets, at any rate, calling down a curse on himself if he should be guilty of those sins, says that worldly glory too would come upon him as the greatest of evils. He speaks thus: “O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is injustice in my hands, if I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, then may I fall away empty before my enemies; may the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the ground, and make my glory dwell in the dust” (Psalm 7:3–5).

Nor, again, are these sayings contrary to the blessings in the Law, which teach that the righteous man eats and is filled (compare Leviticus 26:5; Deuteronomy 11:15): “Do not be anxious about what you will eat or what you will drink. Consider the birds of the air,” or, “Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, and our heavenly Father feeds them. How much more do you surpass the birds?” (Matthew 6:25–26; Luke 12:24), and “Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field” (Matthew 6:28), and what follows. Nor are they contrary to what Solomon said in these words: “A righteous man eats and fills his soul, but the souls of the ungodly are in want” (Proverbs 13:25).

For we must see that the blessing in the Law makes known the food of the soul, with which it is not the composite man that is filled, but the soul alone. From the Gospel, however, we should perhaps take something deeper, and perhaps also something simpler: that one must not let the soul be distracted by cares about food and clothing, but, practising plain living, be confident of being provided for by God, if one takes thought only for what is necessary.

title: Turning the other cheek in the old Scripture
english: Celsus, then, without setting the passages from the Law that seem contrary beside those from the Gospel, also says this: “to let the man who has struck once strike again.” We shall reply that we know the saying “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth,” spoken to the men of old (Matthew 5:38; Exodus 21:24), and that we have also read “But I say to you” (Matthew 5:39): “To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also” (Luke 6:29).

But since Celsus, I think, has had his ears filled by those who divide the deity of the Gospel from the deity of the Law, and so puts forward such things, we must say in answer to his argument that the old writings too know the saying “To the one who strikes you on the right cheek, offer the other also” (Matthew 5:39). At any rate, it is written in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “It is good for a man when he bears a yoke in his youth. He will sit alone and keep silent, because he has taken it upon himself. He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him, and he will be filled with reproaches” (Lamentations 3:27–28, 30).

The Gospel of God does not issue orders contrary to the God of the Law, not even about the blow on the cheek taken literally. Neither of the two is lying, neither Moses nor Jesus; nor did the Father, in sending Jesus, forget what he had commanded Moses; nor indeed did he condemn his own laws, change his mind, and send his messenger for the opposite purpose.

title: Why the law’s commonwealth gave way to the Gospel
english: If we must say at least a little about the difference between the order of life the Jews once followed under Moses and the one Christians now seek to achieve according to the teaching of Jesus, we shall say this. It was not fitting for the calling of the Gentiles, who are placed under the Romans, to live according to the law of Moses taken to the letter; nor, on the other hand, could the Jews of old have kept the structure of their commonwealth intact if, let us suppose, they had obeyed the way of life set by the Gospel.

For Christians could not, according to the law of Moses, put enemies to death, or those who had acted against the law and been judged deserving of death by fire or by stoning; seeing that not even the Jews, though they wish to, are able to carry out these things according to that law, as the law commanded. Again, if you forbid the Jews of that time, who had a commonwealth and a land of their own, to march out against their enemies, to go to war for their ancestral ways, and to put to death or in some way punish those who had committed adultery or murder or done anything like these, nothing is left but for them to be utterly destroyed all at once when their enemies attacked the nation, since their own law would have hamstrung them and prevented them from defending themselves against their enemies.

And providence, which of old gave the Law and now has given the Gospel of Jesus Christ, not wishing the Jewish order to prevail any longer, destroyed their city and their temple, and the service of God that was carried on at the temple through sacrifices and the prescribed worship. And just as, not wishing those things to be carried on any longer, it destroyed them, in the same way it has made the Christian cause grow, and day by day that cause has advanced in numbers and now also in freedom of speech; and this although countless obstacles have arisen to keep the teaching of Jesus from being sown across the world. But since it was God who willed that those from the Gentiles too should be helped by the teaching of Jesus the Christ, every human plan against Christians has been brought down; and the more kings and rulers of nations and peoples everywhere humbled them, the more they multiplied “and grew exceedingly strong” (Exodus 1:7, 12).

title: Christians do not say that God has a body
english: After this, Celsus at some length sets down, as if they were said by us, things about God that we do not say: as though God were by nature a body, and a body of human form. And he wishes to overturn positions we have not laid down, which it is superfluous to quote, or his refutation of them either. For if we said what he claims we assert about God, and he were taking his stand against that, we would have had to set down his words, to establish our own position and to undo his. But if he strings together for himself things that he either heard from no one, or, granting even that he heard them, heard from some simple and guileless people who do not know the intent of our teaching, we need not busy ourselves with what is not necessary.

For our Scriptures plainly say that God is incorporeal. That is why “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18), and “the firstborn of all creation” is said to be “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), as if it said “of the incorporeal God.” We have also dealt with God adequately in what came before, when we examined how we understand “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

title: The better land promised to the righteous
english: After what he says about God, in which he slanders us, he asks us where we expect to go, and what hope we have. And as though we had answered, he sets down supposed words of ours, which run: “To another land, better than this one.” To this he says: “Divine men of old have told of a happy life for happy souls. Some named it the Islands of the Blessed, others the Elysian Plain, from the release from the evils of this world, as Homer too says: ‘But the immortals will send you to the Elysian Plain and the ends of the earth, where life is easiest’ (Homer, Odyssey 4.563–565). And Plato, who holds the soul to be immortal, openly calls that region to which it is sent a ‘land,’ in these words: ‘that it is something very great, and that we who dwell from the Phasis to the Pillars of Heracles inhabit a small part of it, living around the sea like ants or frogs around a marsh, and that many others dwell elsewhere in many such places. For everywhere around the earth there are many hollows of every kind, in shape and in size, into which water, mist and air have flowed together; but the earth itself lies pure in the pure heaven’ (Plato, Phaedo 109a–c).”

Celsus supposes, then, that we have taken what we say about the other land, better than this one and far superior to it, from certain men whom he regards as divine men of old, and above all from Plato, who in the Phaedo discoursed as a philosopher about a pure earth lying in the pure heaven. He does not see that Moses, who is far older even than the writings of the Greeks, brought in God promising the holy land, “good and broad, flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8), to those who had lived according to his law; and not, as some think, promising as the “good” land the Judaea that is reckoned to be here below, which itself also lies within the earth that was cursed from the beginning in the works of Adam’s transgression.

For the words “Cursed is the earth in your works; in sorrows you shall eat of it all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:17) were spoken about the whole earth. Every man who has died “in Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:22) eats of it “in sorrows,” that is, in toils, and he eats of it “all the days of” his “life.” And because the whole earth is “cursed,” it “will bring forth thorns and thistles” (Genesis 3:18) “all the days of the life” of him who was cast out of paradise in Adam (Genesis 3:23–24); and every man eats his bread “in the sweat of” his “face, until he returns to the earth from which he was taken” (Genesis 3:19).

Everything in this passage calls for long discussion, which could be worked out to make its words clear. For the present we have been content with a few remarks, wishing to free from distraction anyone who supposes that what is said about the good land which God promises to the righteous was said about the land of Judaea.

title: The promised land is not Judaea
english: If, then, the whole “earth” is itself “cursed in the works” (Genesis 3:17) of Adam and of those who died in him (1 Corinthians 15:22), it is clear that all its parts share in the curse as well. Among them is the land of Judaea, so that the words “into a good and large land, into a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8) cannot be fitted to it. This holds even if Judaea and Jerusalem are shown to be, in a symbolic way, a shadow of the good and large land, pure and lying in a pure heaven, in which is the heavenly Jerusalem. Of this Jerusalem the apostle speaks as one who had been raised together with Christ and was seeking the things above (Colossians 3:1), and who had found a meaning bound to no Jewish fable. He says: “But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering” (Hebrews 12:22).

So that anyone may be persuaded that what we say about the good and large land in Moses is not contrary to the intention of the divine Spirit, let him give his attention to all the prophets. They teach the return to Jerusalem of those who have wandered and fallen away from it, and, in a word, of those who are being restored to what is called the place and city of God in the words of the one who said, “His place is in holy peace” (Psalm 76:2), and who also says, “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, on his holy mountain, well rooted, with the joy of the whole earth” (Psalm 48:1–2).

But for the present it is enough to set out the words of the thirty-sixth Psalm (Psalm 37), which speak thus about the land of the righteous: “But those who wait for the Lord, they shall inherit the land” (Psalm 37:9); and a little after, “But the meek shall inherit the land and delight in abundance of peace” (Psalm 37:11); and a little after, “Those who bless him shall inherit the land” (Psalm 37:22); and again, “The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it for ever and ever” (Psalm 37:29). And see whether, to those who are able to hear these words in the same Psalm, it is not made plain that the earth is pure in the pure heaven: “Wait for the Lord and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the land” (Psalm 37:34).

title: Plato’s precious stones and the city in Isaiah
english: It seems to me that what Plato says about the stones thought precious here, which are said to have a kind of outflow from the stones in the better earth, was also taken from what is recorded in Isaiah about the city of God. Of that city it is written: “I will make your battlements jasper, and your stones stones of crystal, and your enclosing wall choice stones” (Isaiah 54:12); and again, “I will make your foundations sapphire” (Isaiah 54:11).

Now those who have taken the philosopher’s words in a loftier sense expound the myth in Plato allegorically. As for the prophecies, from which we conjecture that Plato too borrowed, they will be explained by those who have lived as kin to the prophets and filled with God, and who have given all their time to the study of the sacred writings; and they will explain them to those who are fitted for it by purity of life and by love of learning about divine things.

Our own aim was to show that we did not take what we say about the holy land from the Greeks or from Plato. They, rather, being later not only than Moses, the most ancient of all, but also than most of the prophets, either misheard certain people who spoke in riddles about such things, or else came upon the sacred Scriptures and, altering what they found on these matters, said things of this kind about the better earth. Haggai shows clearly that “the dry land” is one thing and “the earth” another, giving the name dry land to this ground on which we are. He speaks thus: “Once more I will shake the heaven and the earth and the dry land and the sea” (Haggai 2:6).

title: True realities bear the names of earthly things
english: Celsus himself puts off the explanation of the myth in Plato, which is found in the Phaedo, saying: “What he means to show by these words is not easy for everyone to know, unless one were able to understand what it is that he says: ‘through weakness and slowness we are not able to pass through to the uttermost air’; and ‘if one’s nature were able to bear the sight, one would know that that is the true heaven and the true light’ (Plato, Phaedo 109d–110a).” In the same way we too, thinking that it does not belong to the present treatise to make clear what concerns the holy and good land and the city of God in it, put this off to our commentaries on the prophets. We have already given a partial account, as far as we could, of the city of God in what we have written on the forty-fifth Psalm and the forty-seventh Psalm (Psalms 46 and 48).

The most ancient teaching of Moses and the prophets knows that all the true things bear the same names as the more common things here. For example, it speaks of a “true light” (John 1:9), and a “heaven” other than “the firmament” (Genesis 1:1, 1:8), and a sun “of righteousness” (Malachi 4:2) other than the sun we perceive with the senses. And, in a word, to set them apart from the things of sense, none of which is true, it says: “God, true are his works” (Deuteronomy 32:4). It applies the name “works of God” to some things, and the so-called “works of his hands” to lesser ones. At any rate, when it reproaches certain people through Isaiah, it says: “They do not look upon the works of the Lord, and they do not consider the works of his hands” (Isaiah 5:12). So much for this.

title: Resurrection, not transmigration
english: The doctrine of the resurrection is large and hard to explain. If any doctrine needs a wise man, and one far advanced, it needs one to set forth what is worthy of God and the grandeur of the doctrine, which teaches that what the Scriptures call the tent of the soul has the character of a seed: the tent in which the righteous groan, being burdened, not wishing to put it off but to put on over it (2 Corinthians 5:4). Celsus did not understand this doctrine; because he heard about it from unlearned people who could not set it forth with any reasoning, he mocks what is said. So, in addition to what we said about it earlier, it is useful to note only this in reply to his argument: we do not speak of resurrection, as Celsus thinks, because we have misheard the doctrine of transmigration of souls.

We speak of it because we know that the soul, which in its own nature is bodiless and invisible, when it is in any bodily place, needs a body suited to the nature of that place. This body it wears, at times having stripped off what was necessary before but is superfluous for its second state, and at times having put it on over what it had before, since it needs a better garment for the purer, ethereal, and heavenly places. So, when it came to birth here, it put off the membrane that was useful for its life in the womb of the mother who carried it, while it was there; and beneath that it had put on what was necessary for one who was to live on earth.

Then again, since there is a “tent” with an earthly house that is in some way necessary to the tent, the Scriptures say that the earthly house “of the tent” is dissolved, but that the tent puts on over itself “a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1). And the men of God say that “the perishable” puts on “imperishability,” which differs from the imperishable, and that “the mortal” puts on “immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53), which is something other than the immortal. For as wisdom is related to the wise, and righteousness to the righteous, and peace to the peaceful, so imperishability is related to the imperishable, and immortality to the immortal. See, then, to what the passage urges us, when it speaks of putting on imperishability and immortality. Like garments on one who has put them on and is wrapped in them, these do not allow the one who wears them to perish or die.
We have ventured even this much because of the man who did not understand what we mean by the resurrection, and for that reason laughs and mocks at a doctrine he does not know.

title: God is known by the mind and seen by a pure heart
english: Supposing that we hold the doctrine of the resurrection for the sake of knowing and seeing God, Celsus strings together whatever he likes, and says something like this: “When they are shut out on every side and refuted, they come back again, as if they had heard nothing, to the same question: ‘How then are we to know and see God? And how are we to go to him?’”

Let anyone who wishes know, then, that even if for other purposes we need a body, because we are in a bodily place, and a body suited to the nature of that bodily place, and even if, since we need the body, we put on over the tent what we have described, yet for the knowledge of God we have no need of a body at all. For what knows God is not the eye of the body but the mind, which sees what is “in the image” (Genesis 1:26–27) of the Creator, and which by the providence of God has received the power to know God.

And what sees God is a pure heart, from which there no longer “come forth evil thoughts,” no “murders,” no “adulteries,” no “fornications,” no “thefts,” no “false witness,” no “blasphemies” (Matthew 15:19), no “evil eye” (Mark 7:22), nor anything else that is wrong. That is why it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). But since our own free choice is not enough for us to have a heart wholly “pure,” and we need God to create it so, the one who prays with understanding says: “Create in me a pure heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10).

title: Spiritual eyes, ears, and hands
english: But neither shall we ask anyone, as though God were in a place, and say: “How are we to go to him?” For God is greater than every place and contains all things whatever, and there is nothing that contains God. So the command given us, “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 13:4), does not tell us to go to God in a bodily way; nor is it in a bodily way that the prophet, who clung to God, says in his prayer: “My soul has clung close after you” (Psalm 63:8).

Celsus, then, lies about us when he says that we expect to see God with the eyes of the body, to hear his voice with our ears, and to touch him with hands perceptible to the senses. But we know that the divine words speak of eyes that bear the same name as the eyes of the body, and likewise of ears and of hands, and, what is more surprising still, of a sense more divine than, and different in kind from, the one that most people ordinarily call by that name.

For when the prophet says, “Uncover my eyes, and I will consider your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18), or, “The commandment of the Lord shines far, giving light to the eyes” (Psalm 19:8), or, “Give light to my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Psalm 13:3), no one is so dull-witted as to think that “the wonders” of the divine “law” are perceived with the eyes of the body, or that the Lord’s commandment gives light to the eyes of the body, or that the sleep that brings on death befalls the eyes of the body.

Again, when our Saviour says, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8), even an ordinary person understands that this is said of more divine ears. And when it is said that “the word of the Lord” came “by the hand” of Jeremiah the prophet (Jeremiah 37:2), or of someone else (Haggai 1:1), or that the law came “by the hand” of Moses (Leviticus 26:46), or, “With my hands I sought God, and I was not deceived” (Psalm 77:2), no one is so foolish as not to take it that there are hands so called in a figurative sense. Of these John too says: “Our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1).
And if you wish to learn from the sacred writings about the better sense as well, the one that is not bodily, hear Solomon saying in Proverbs: “You will find a divine sense” (Proverbs 2:5).

title: Oracles of demons and the risen Jesus
english: We have no need, then, since we seek God in this way, to go off where Celsus sends us, to Trophonius, to Amphiaraus and to Mopsus, where he says gods in human form are to be seen, and, as Celsus puts it, “not deceptive but even plainly visible.” For we know that these are demons, fed on the savour of burnt fat, on blood, and on the fumes that rise from the sacrifices, and so held fast in prisons built from their own craving; these the Greeks have taken to be temples of gods. But we know that such places are the dwellings of deceiving demons.

After this Celsus speaks with malice about the gods in human form already mentioned, as he calls them, saying that one will see them “not slipping by once, like the one who deceived these people, but always conversing with any who wish.” By these words he seems to have thought that Jesus, who appeared to his disciples after his resurrection from the dead, was a phantom, as though he had slipped by in order to be seen by them; while those he named gods in human form he supposes to converse always with any who wish.

But how can a phantom which, as he himself says, slipped by to deceive those who saw it, go on after that sight to accomplish so much, to turn the souls of such people, and to persuade them that they must do everything in a way pleasing to God, as men who will be judged? And how does what he calls a phantom drive out demons and perform other works not to be despised, not confined to one allotted place, as his gods in human form are, but reaching through the whole inhabited world, and by its own divinity gathering and drawing all whom it finds to have turned themselves toward the good life?

title: Words put in Christian mouths
english: After this, which we have answered as well as we could, Celsus again says something like this: “And again they will say: ‘How will they know God if they do not grasp him by sense? What can be learned without sense?’” Then, in answer to this, he says: “This is the voice not of a man, nor of the soul, but of the flesh. Still, let them hear, if they can understand anything at all, cowardly and body-loving race that they are. If you close off sense and look up with the mind, and turn from the flesh and rouse the eyes of the soul, only so will you see God. And if you seek a guide for this way, you must flee the deceivers and sorcerers and those who woo men to idols, so that you may not be utterly ridiculous, blaspheming as idols the other gods, the ones that are displayed, while you worship one more wretched even than the real idols, no longer even an idol but in truth a dead man, and seek a father like him.”

First we must say, in reply to the speech he composes in our name, putting into our mouths words as though we spoke them in defence of the resurrection of the flesh, that the merit of one who writes a speech in another’s character is to keep the purpose and the character of the person represented, and the fault is to put into the speaker’s mouth words that do not fit him. Equally to blame are those who, in such speeches, put philosophy into the mouths of barbarians and uneducated people, or of household slaves, who have never heard philosophical discourse nor ever spoken it well: philosophy which the writer has learned, but which the character represented could not be expected to know. Equally to blame, again, are those who put into the mouths of characters presented in the story as wise and as knowing divine things the kind of words that uneducated people say from common passions and utter out of ignorance.

That is why Homer is admired in many places, for keeping the characters of his heroes as he set them up from the beginning, such as that of Nestor, or Odysseus, or Diomedes, or Agamemnon, or Telemachus, or Penelope, or any of the rest; while Euripides is mocked in comedy by Aristophanes as one who speaks out of season, because he often put speeches about doctrines he had learned from Anaxagoras or from one of the other wise men into the mouths of barbarian women or of slaves.

title: A speech that fits no Christian
english: If, then, such is the merit in writing speeches for characters and such the fault, who could not laugh at Celsus, and with good reason, when he puts into the mouths of Christians things that Christians do not say? For if he was making up the words of simple folk, how could such people distinguish sense from mind and the objects of sense from the objects of thought, and teach, like the Stoics who do away with intelligible realities, that whatever is grasped is grasped by the senses and that all grasping depends on the senses? But if he is making up the words of those who study philosophy and who examine carefully, as far as they are able, the things of Christ, he has not given them words that fit them either.

For no one who has learned that God is invisible, and that there are some invisible created things, that is, intelligible ones (Colossians 1:15–16), would say, as though in defence of the resurrection: “How will they know God if they do not grasp him by the senses?” or “What can be learned without sense?” And it is written, not in writings kept apart and read only by a few lovers of learning, but in the more commonly read ones, that “the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Romans 1:20). From this we may know that, even if people in this life must begin from the senses and the objects of sense when they are going to rise up to the nature of intelligible things, they must certainly not remain among the objects of sense. Nor will they say that it is impossible to learn intelligible things without sense; and if they do use the words “Who can learn without sense?”, they will show that Celsus had no good reason to add to them “the voice not of a man, nor of the soul, but of the flesh.”

title: God known by the mind made in his image
english: We say, then, that the God of the universe is mind, or beyond mind and being, simple, invisible and without body; and so we would say that God is grasped by nothing other than by what has been made in the image of that mind (Genesis 1:27). Now, to use Paul’s words, it is “through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). And if I say “face,” let no one misrepresent, because of the word, the sense it conveys. Let him learn instead from the words “with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18), that in such places it is not a face of the senses that is meant, but one understood figuratively, like the eyes and ears and all the other things we showed above to share their names with the members of the body.

Man, then, that is, the soul using a body, which is called “the inner man” (Romans 7:22; Ephesians 3:16) and also “soul,” answers not what Celsus wrote down but what the man of God himself teaches. A Christian would not use the voice of the flesh, since he has learned “by the Spirit to put to death the deeds of the body” (Romans 8:13), and “always to carry about in the body the dying of Jesus” (2 Corinthians 4:10), and “Put to death the members that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:5). He knows what is meant by “My Spirit shall not remain in these men for ever, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3); he understands too that “those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8:8); and for this reason he does everything so as no longer to be at all “in the flesh, but” only “in the Spirit” (Romans 8:9).

title: The two kinds of eyes
english: Let us see, too, what he calls us to, so that we may hear from him in what way we shall know God. Here he thinks that no Christian can understand what he says, for he says: “Still, let them hear, if they can understand anything at all.” We must consider, then, what words of his he wants us to hear. The philosopher, who ought to teach us, rails at us instead; and whereas he ought to show his goodwill toward his hearers at the opening of his discourse, he calls “a cowardly race” those who go as far as death rather than renounce Christianity even in a word, and who are ready for every torment and every kind of death. He also says that we are “a body-loving race,” we who say, “Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Corinthians 5:16), and who lay down the body for godliness so readily that a philosopher would not take off even his cloak as easily.

He says to us, then: “If you close off the senses and look up with the mind, and turn from the flesh and rouse the eye of the soul, only so will you see God.” And he thinks that this (I mean the teaching about two kinds of eyes), which he took from the Greeks, had not already been taught as philosophy among us. We must say that Moses, writing the account of the world’s making, presents man before the transgression as in one way seeing and in another not seeing. He was seeing, in what is said about the woman: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasing to the eyes to look at, and beautiful to contemplate” (Genesis 3:6). He was not seeing, not only in the serpent’s words to the woman, spoken as though about blind eyes, “For God knew that on the day you eat of it your eyes will be opened” (Genesis 3:5), but also in the words “They ate, and the eyes of the two were opened” (Genesis 3:6–7).

So it was the eyes of sense that were “opened,” which they had done well to keep closed, so that they would not be distracted and hindered from seeing with the eye of the soul. But the eyes of the soul, which until then had been seeing and rejoicing in God and in his paradise, these, I think, they closed because of their sin. That is why our Saviour too, knowing that we have this twofold kind of eyes, says: “For judgement I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). By “those who do not see” he hints at the eyes of the soul, which the Word makes see; by “those who see,” at the eyes of the senses; and these the Word blinded, so that the soul might see without distraction what it ought.

In everyone, therefore, who lives as a Christian in the right way, the eye of the soul has been roused and the eye of sense has been closed; and in proportion to the rousing of the better eye and the closing of the eyes of sense, the God over all, and his Son, who is Word and Wisdom and all the rest, are understood and beheld by each.

title: Celsus confuses Christians with the Ophites
english: After the passages we have examined, Celsus directs a speech as though to all Christians. If it was fitting to say it at all, it should have been said to those who admit that they are wholly foreign to the teaching of Jesus.
