For the Ophites, as we said earlier, who deny Jesus outright, or any others who think as they do, are the ones who traffic in idols, the deceivers and sorcerers; and they are the ones who wretchedly learn by heart the names of the doorkeepers. It is idle, then, for him to say to Christians: “And if you seek a guide for this road, you must shun the deceivers and sorcerers and those who traffic in idols.”

He does not even know that such men, sorcerers as they are, speak evil of Jesus and of all the worship of God that he taught, no less than Celsus does and together with him. Mixing us up with them in his own argument, he says: “so that you may not be utterly ridiculous, blaspheming the others, the gods that are displayed, as idols, while you revere one who is more wretched even than what are truly idols, and no longer even an idol but really a corpse, and seek a father like him.”

For that he does not know what Christians say and what is said by those who invent such myths, but supposes that the charges brought against them belong to us, and so says to us things that do not apply to us, is plain from these words: “This kind of deceit, then, and those wonderful counsellors, and the demonic words addressed to the lion, and to the amphibious one, and to the ass-shaped one, and to the others, and the marvellous doorkeepers, whose names you poor wretches learn by heart to your misery, and are grievously possessed and impaled.”

He did not see that none of those who believe that the lion-shaped, the ass-shaped and the amphibious one are doorkeepers of the ascent stands firm to the point of death, even for what seems to him to be the truth. But what we do from an excess of piety, if I may put it so, when we offer ourselves to every kind of death, and being impaled as well, he attaches to those who suffer none of these things; and to us, who are impaled for the sake of piety, he makes a reproach of their myth-making about the lion-shaped one, the amphibious one and the rest. It is not, then, because of Celsus that we shun the teaching about the lion-shaped one and the rest, for we never received any such thing to begin with. Rather, following the teaching of Jesus, we say the opposite of what they say, and we do not accept that Michael has a face of this sort, or some other of those listed earlier a face of that sort.

title: Which ancient guides should we follow?
english: We must consider whom Celsus wants us to follow, as though we shall not be at a loss for ancient guides and holy men. He sends us back to “inspired poets”, as he calls them, and to “wise men and philosophers”, without giving them names; and though he promises to show us the guides, he speaks in vague terms of “the inspired poets and wise men and philosophers”. If he had given the names of each of them, it would have seemed reasonable for us to contend that he gives us guides who are blind about the truth, so that we should go astray; or, if not wholly blind, at least mistaken about many doctrines of the truth.

Whether, then, he means that Orpheus is an inspired poet, or Parmenides, or Empedocles, or even Homer himself, or Hesiod, let whoever wishes show how those who use such guides travel the road better, and are more helped in the conduct of life, than those who, through the teaching of Jesus Christ, have left behind all statues and images, and indeed all Jewish superstition too, and who, through the Word of God, look up to God alone, the Father of the Word.

And who are the wise men or the philosophers from whom Celsus wants us to hear “many divine things”? Are we to leave behind Moses, the servant of God (Numbers 12:7), and the prophets of the Maker of the universe, who in truth have spoken numberless things by inspiration? And are we to leave him who shone upon the human race and proclaimed the way of the worship of God, and who, as far as lay in him, left no one without a taste of his own mysteries? Rather, through his surpassing love for mankind he is able to give the more intelligent a theology that can lift the soul up from the things of this world; and yet no less does he come down also to the lower capacities of unlearned men and simpler women and slaves, and, in a word, of those whom no one helped but Jesus alone, so that they might live better, as far as they could, with such doctrines about God as they were able to receive.

title: Plato’s hidden maker and the Word made flesh
english: Then, after this, he sends us back to Plato as to a more effective teacher of the things of theology, and sets out his words from the Timaeus, which run as follows: “Now to find the maker and father of this universe is a hard task, and having found him, it is impossible to declare him to all” (Plato, Timaeus 28c). Then he adds to these words, saying: “You see how the way of truth too is sought by seers, and how Plato knew that to walk this way is ‘impossible’ for all. But since, for this reason, wise men have devised a means by which we might grasp some idea of the Nameless and First, one that makes him plain either by synthesis applied to other things, or by analysis from them, or by analogy, and since I wish to teach what is otherwise beyond speech, I should be surprised if you were able to follow, bound as you are wholly to the flesh and seeing nothing pure.”

Plato, indeed, puts forward the passage set out above in a lofty way, and one not to be despised. But see whether the divine word does not show greater love for mankind when it presents God the Word, who was “in the beginning with God” (John 1:2), becoming flesh (John 1:14), so that the Word might be able to reach all: the very Word of whom Plato says that, for one who has found him, it is “impossible to declare him to all”.

Let Plato say, then, that “to find the maker and father of this universe” is “a hard task”, showing that it is “impossible” for human nature to find God as he deserves, or, if not as he deserves, at least more fully than the many do. If this were true, and God had in truth been found by Plato or by any of the Greeks, they would not have revered something else and called it god and bowed down to it, either abandoning him or taking alongside him things that may not be taken alongside so great a God.

But we declare that human nature is not sufficient in any way at all to seek God and find him purely, unless it is helped by the One it seeks. He is found by those who, after doing what lies in their power, confess that they need him, and he shows himself to those to whom he judges it reasonable to be seen (Wisdom of Solomon 1:2), so far as it is natural for God to be known by man, and for the soul of man, while it is still in a body, to know God.

title: He who has seen me has seen the Father
english: Moreover, when Plato says that “having found” “the maker and father of the universe”, it is “impossible to declare him to all”, he does not say that he is beyond speech and nameless, but that, being expressible, he can be spoken of to a few. Then Celsus, as though he had forgotten the words of Plato that he quoted, says that God is nameless, in these words: “But since, for this reason, wise men have devised a means by which we might grasp some idea of the Nameless and First.”

We, however, say that not only God is beyond speech, but also other things that come after him. Paul, straining to point to these, says: “He heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2 Corinthians 12:4). He uses “heard” in place of “understood”, as in the saying, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8; Matthew 11:15).

As for “the maker and father of the universe”, we say that to see him is “a hard task”. Yet he is seen, not only in keeping with the words, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), but also in keeping with what is said by the image “of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15): “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me” (John 14:9; John 12:45). For no one with any sense would say that in these words Jesus was referring to his body, which could be perceived by the senses and was visible to men, when he said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me.” For on that reading all who said, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23:21), would have seen God the Father, and so would Pilate, who received authority over his human nature; and that is absurd.

That the words “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me” are not to be taken in the commoner sense is clear from what was said to Philip: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?” (John 14:9). He said this to him when he made the request, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8). Whoever, then, has understood how we must take what is said about the only-begotten God (John 1:18), the Son of God, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), inasmuch as “the Word” became “flesh” (John 1:14), will see how anyone who has seen the image “of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15) will know “the Father and maker of this universe”.

title: Knowledge of God is a gift of grace
english: Celsus, then, thinks that God is known either by synthesis applied to other things, like what geometers call synthesis, or by analysis from other things, or else by analogy, like the analogy the same geometers use; if, that is, anyone can come in this way to the threshold of the Good (Plato, Philebus 64c). But the Word of God, who said, “No one has known the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son reveals him” (Matthew 11:27), declares that God is known by a divine grace, which comes to be in the soul not without God, but with a kind of inspiration.

For it is likely that the knowledge of God is greater than human nature can reach, which is why there are so many errors among men about God; but that, by the goodness and love for mankind of God, and by a wonderful and more divine grace, the knowledge of God reaches those whom God, in his foreknowledge, has laid hold of beforehand as people who would live worthily of him whom they have come to know. They would never debase their piety toward him, not even if they were led away to death by those who do not know what piety is, and who make anything at all out to be piety rather than what piety really is; nor even if they were thought to be the most ridiculous of men.

God, I think, also saw the arrogance, or the contempt for others, of those who pride themselves on having known God and on having learned divine things from philosophy, yet who, like the most ignorant, turn to statues and their temples and the much-talked-of mysteries. And so he “chose the foolish things of the world” (1 Corinthians 1:27), the simplest among Christians, who live more temperately and more purely than many philosophers, “to put to shame the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27), who are not ashamed to converse with lifeless things as with gods or images of gods.

For who that has sense will not laugh at a man who, after all the great and numerous discourses in philosophy about God or gods, gazes at statues, and either sends up his prayer to them, or, through the sight of them, carries it up from what is seen, which is a symbol, to the being known by the mind, to whom he fancies he must ascend? But the Christian, even the unlearned one, is convinced that every place in the world is a part of the whole, since the whole world is God’s temple. Praying “in every place” (1 Timothy 2:8), and closing the eyes of sense and raising those of the soul, he rises above the whole world.

He does not even stop at the vault of heaven, but, coming in thought to the place above the heavens (Plato, Phaedrus 247b-c), led by the divine Spirit, and being as it were outside the world, he sends up to God a prayer that is not about ordinary things. For he has learned from Jesus to seek nothing small, that is, nothing that the senses perceive, but only the great and truly divine things (compare Matthew 6:33), which, given by God, help a man on his way to the blessedness that is with him, through his Son, who is the Word and God.

title: Celsus borrows Plato’s sun
english: Let us see also what he says he will teach us, if indeed we shall be able to follow it. Here he says that we are bound fast to the flesh altogether, we who, if we live rightly and in keeping with the word of Jesus, hear the saying: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Romans 8:9). He says too that we see nothing pure, we who try to keep even our thoughts from being defiled by the promptings of wickedness, and who say in prayer, “Create a pure heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit in my inmost parts” (Psalm 51:10), so that with the “pure heart” (Matthew 5:8), which alone is by nature able to see God, we may behold him.

What he says is this: “Being and becoming: the intelligible, the visible. With being goes truth; with becoming, error. Knowledge, then, is concerned with truth, and opinion with the other (compare Plato, Republic 534a; Timaeus 29c). Of the intelligible there is thought, of the visible, sight; mind knows the intelligible, and the eye the visible. What the sun is, then, among visible things, being neither eye nor sight, but the cause to the eye of its seeing, to sight of its existing through the sun, to visible things of their being seen, to all things perceived by sense of their coming into being, and indeed to itself of its being beheld, that is what he is among intelligible things, he who is neither mind nor thought nor knowledge, but is the cause to mind of its thinking, to thought of its existing through him, to knowledge of its knowing through him, and to all intelligible things, to truth itself and to being itself, of their being; he is beyond all things, and is known by the mind through a certain unspeakable power (Plato, Republic 508b-509b). These things have been said for men who have intelligence; and if you too understand any of them, it is well with you. And if you think that some spirit comes down from God to foretell divine things, this would be the spirit that proclaims these things, the spirit with which men of old were filled when they announced many good things. If you cannot grasp them, keep silent and cover up your own ignorance, and do not say that those who see are blind and that those who run are lame, when you yourselves are lamed and maimed in your souls in every way, and live by the body, that is, by what is dead.”

title: Who has truly lamed the soul
english: To this we shall reply as men who have made it our practice to be hostile to nothing that is well said, and, even when those outside the faith speak well, not to quarrel with them or to seek to overturn what is sound. There are those who revile men who wish, as far as they are able, to be devout toward the God of all, the God who accepts the faith of the simple in him and the reasoned piety of the more intelligent toward him, as they send up prayers with thanksgiving to the Maker of all, and send them up as through a high priest who set pure reverence for God before men. These men call them lame and maimed in their souls, and they say that those who make it their practice to say from the heart, “For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty for God” (2 Corinthians 10:3–4), live by the body, a dead thing. Let them see to it that, in this very act of speaking ill of men who pray to be God’s, they do not make their own souls lame and maim their own “inner man” (Romans 7:22), cutting away from it the gentleness and steadiness that the Creator has naturally sown in rational nature, through their slanders against others, men who wish to live well.

But those who, besides other things, have learned from the divine word, and practise, to bless “when reviled,” to endure “when persecuted,” and to entreat “when slandered” (1 Corinthians 4:12–13), these would be the ones who have set the feet of the soul upright, and who are cleansing and making ready the whole soul. They do so not in order to separate, in words alone, being from becoming and the intelligible from the visible, joining truth to being and fleeing in every way the error that goes with becoming; rather, as they have learned, they look not at the things of becoming, which are “seen” and therefore “temporary,” but at the better things (2 Corinthians 4:18), whether one wishes to call them being, or “invisible” because they are intelligible, or “not seen” because their nature lies beyond the senses.

And the disciples of Jesus look at the things of becoming too, but in such a way as to use them as a kind of stepping-stone to the contemplation of the nature of intelligible things. For “the invisible things” of God, that is, the intelligible things, “from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Romans 1:20); they are seen in being understood. And when they have climbed up from the created things of the world, they do not stop at the invisible things of God; but after exercising themselves enough in these and understanding them, they rise to the eternal power of God and, in a word, to his divinity (Romans 1:20). They know that God in his love for mankind “manifested” “the truth” and “what can be known” of himself (Romans 1:18–19), not only to those devoted to him, but also to some who are outside pure reverence for God and piety toward him; but that some of those who by the providence of God had climbed up to the knowledge of such great things do what is unworthy of that knowledge, act impiously, and “hold down the truth in unrighteousness” (Romans 1:18), and can no longer have even room for a defence before God, since they had knowledge of such great things (Romans 1:20).

title: Philosophers who knew God and bowed to images
english: At any rate, the divine word bears witness about those who grasped what Celsus sets out and who profess to practise philosophy by these doctrines, that “although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasonings, and,” after so great a light of knowledge about what God had manifested to them, “their senseless heart,” for all its eagerness, “was darkened” (Romans 1:21). One can see, indeed, how those “who claim to be wise” (Romans 1:22) display signs of great folly, when, after such great discourses in their schools about God and the intelligible things, “they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things” (Romans 1:23).

And so they themselves, abandoned by providence as men who had not lived worthily of what God had manifested to them, wallow “in the lusts of their hearts, to uncleanness” (Romans 1:24), and “their bodies are dishonoured” (Romans 1:24) in indecencies and licentiousness, because they “exchanged the truth of God for the lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25).

title: Purity without hemlock
english: But those whom they despise for lack of learning, and call fools and slaves, even if all they do is entrust themselves to God, have received the teaching of Jesus and stand so far from licentiousness and uncleanness and every indecency in sexual relations that many of them, after the manner of perfect priests who have turned away from all sexual intercourse, keep themselves wholly pure, and not only from every act of union.

At Athens, I suppose, there is one hierophant who, not trusting himself to be master of his male desires and able to control them as far as he wishes, has his male parts treated with hemlock, and is then thought pure for the worship that is customary among the Athenians. But among Christians one can see men who have had no need of hemlock in order to serve the Divine purely, but who are content with the word instead of hemlock, so that, having driven every desire out of their minds, they serve the Divine with prayers.

In the service of others who are reckoned to be gods there are virgins, very easily counted, whether they are guarded by men or not (for it is not our purpose now to examine that), who seem to remain in purity for the sake of the honour paid to the deity. But among Christians it is not for honours from men, not for wages and money, nor for a scrap of glory, that they practise perfect virginity; and as “they saw fit to keep God in their knowledge” (compare Romans 1:28), they are kept by God in an approved mind and in “doing what is fitting,” filled with all righteousness and goodness (compare Romans 1:28–29).

title: Simple believers who live better
english: I have said these things not out of any wish to quarrel with what has been well conceived among the Greeks too, nor to find fault with sound doctrines, but because I wish to show that these things, and things even greater and more divine than these, have been said by the divine men, the prophets of God and the apostles of Jesus, and are searched out by those who wish to be Christians more perfectly and who know that “the mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment; the law of his God is in his heart” (Psalm 37:30–31).

And even among those to whom these things have not been made clear, whether through great lack of learning, or through simplicity, or through want of anyone to urge them on toward a reasoned piety, but by whom the God over all is believed in, and his “only-begotten Son” (John 3:18), Word and God, there may be found a plainness and simplicity of dignity, purity and character that is often better. Without it, those “who claim to be wise” (Romans 1:22) wallow with boys in what is unlawful, “men with men committing what is shameful” (Romans 1:27).

title: The error that comes with birth
english: He, then, did not make clear how error goes with becoming, nor did he set out whatever he meant, so that we might understand it by comparing his views with ours. But the prophets, hinting at some wise teaching about the things of becoming, say that a sacrifice “for sin” is offered even for those just born, as not pure from sin (Leviticus 12:6–8). They also say: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 51:5). And they declare as well that “sinners were estranged from the womb,” and they also say, in a surprising way, “they went astray from the belly, they spoke lies” (Psalm 58:3).

So thoroughly do the wise men among us disparage the whole nature of things perceived by the senses that in one place bodies are called vanity, in the words “For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope” (Romans 8:20), and in another they are called the vanity “of vanities,” as the Preacher said: “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). And who has so disparaged the life of the human soul here as he who said, “Nevertheless, all things are vanity, every man living” (Psalm 39:5)? For he had no doubt about the difference between the soul’s life here and its life outside the things of this world, nor did he say, “Who knows whether to live is to die, and to die is to live?” (Euripides, quoted in Plato, Gorgias 492e). Rather, he is bold to speak the truth in the words “our soul was brought low to the dust” (Psalm 44:25) and “you brought me down into the dust of death” (Psalm 22:15).

In keeping with this it has been said, “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24), and also, “who will transform the body of our lowliness” (Philippians 3:21). He too is a prophet who said, “You brought us low in a place of affliction” (Psalm 44:19), calling the region about the earth a “place of affliction,” the place to which Adam, that is, man, came when he was cast out of paradise because of wickedness (Genesis 3:23–24). And as for him who says, “Now we see through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12), and further, “While we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6), and therefore “we are well pleased to be away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8), see how great were the things he had contemplated about the different life of souls.

title: The Spirit given in different measure
english: And why should I go on setting parallels against Celsus’s text, since these things were said among us long before, and our meaning is already plain from what has been said? In these words he also, as it were, grants that if a divine spirit coming down from God foretells divine things, “this would be the spirit that proclaims these teachings, filled with which men of old announced many good things.” But he did not see the distinction carefully drawn among us by those who say that “your incorruptible Spirit is in all things; therefore” God corrects “little by little those who go astray” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:1–2), and who also say, among other things, that “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22) shows a different measure of what is given from the one shown by “You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1:5).

It takes real effort, once these things have been carefully understood, to see the difference between those who, at long intervals, received a grasp of the truth and a brief notion of God, and those who were more fully inspired by God, who always stood with God, and who were at all times led by the divine Spirit. Had Celsus examined and understood this, he would not have charged us with “ignorance”, nor would he have told us not to call blind those who think they show their piety in the material crafts of men, the crafts that make statues. For no one who sees with the eyes of the soul worships the Divine in any other way than the way that shows us how always to keep our eyes on the Maker of the universe, to offer every prayer to him, and to do everything as in the sight of God, as before a spectator who sees even into our thoughts.

We, then, pray both to see and to be guides of the blind (Romans 2:19), until they come to the Word of God and recover the eyes of their soul, which ignorance has blinded. And if we also act worthily of him who said to the disciples, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14), and of the word that taught that “the light shines in the darkness” (John 1:5), we shall also be “a light” to those in darkness (Romans 2:19), and we shall train the foolish and teach the immature (Romans 2:20).

title: Who is lame and who runs
english: Celsus must not be indignant when we call lame, crippled in the feet of the soul, those who hurry to the places reputed to be sacred as though they were truly sacred, and who do not see that no work of artisans can be sacred. But those who are devout according to the teaching of Jesus also run, until, having reached the end of the race, they say in a strong and truthful frame of mind: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; from now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Timothy 4:7–8). And each of us runs in this way, “not aimlessly”, and boxes against wickedness in this way, “not as one beating the air” (1 Corinthians 9:26), but beating those who are under “the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience” (Ephesians 2:2).

Let Celsus say that we “live by the dead body”, we who hear, “If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13), and who learn, “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25). And may we show by our deeds that the one who says of us that we live by the dead body is lying.

title: Celsus offers other heroes
english: Next, after these remarks, which we have answered as well as we could, he says to us: “How much better would it have been for you, since you wanted to make some innovation, to have devoted yourselves to someone else among those who died nobly and who could lend themselves to a divine legend? Come, if Heracles and Asclepius and those glorified of old did not please you, you had Orpheus, a man who by common consent had a holy spirit, and who himself also died a violent death. But perhaps others had already claimed him. Anaxarchus, then: thrown into a mortar and pounded in the most lawless way, he utterly scorned the punishment and said, ‘Pound, pound the bag of Anaxarchus; for you are not pounding the man himself.’ Truly the voice of some divine spirit!

“But here too some natural philosophers got there first and followed him. Epictetus, then? When his master was twisting his leg, he smiled and, quite unshaken, said, ‘You will break it’; and when the master had broken it, he said, ‘Did I not tell you that you would break it?’ What did your God say that was like this, while he was being punished? You would even have had more reason to put forward the Sibyl, whom some of you use, as a child of God. As it is, you can recklessly slip many blasphemous things into her writings, yet you set up as God a man whose life was most infamous and whose death was most pitiable. How much more suitable for you than he would Jonah have been, Jonah ‘with the gourd’ (Jonah 4:6), or Daniel, who came out from the beasts (Daniel 6:23), or others still more fantastic than these?”

title: Celsus’s heroes weighed
english: Since, then, he sends us back to Heracles, let him set before us records of Heracles’ sayings, and let him defend his unseemly slavery in the house of Omphale. Let him show whether divine honour was due to the one who took the farmer’s ox by force, like a robber, feasted on it, and enjoyed the curses the farmer called down on him as he ate; so that even to this day the demon of Heracles is said to receive its sacrifice with curses. He also calls us to repeat ourselves about Asclepius, though we have already spoken about him; but we are content with what we said there.

And what did he admire in Orpheus, that he says that he “by common consent had a holy spirit” and lived a good life? I should be surprised if Celsus too, who now sings the praises of Orpheus out of rivalry with us and in order to belittle Jesus, did not turn away from his poems when he came upon his impious myths about the gods, as deserving to be banished from the good state even more than the poems of Homer (Plato, Republic 398a, 607a). For Orpheus said far worse things than Homer about the so-called gods.

Anaxarchus, to be sure, was noble when he said to Aristocreon, the tyrant of Cyprus, “Pound, pound the bag of Anaxarchus.” But this is the one thing about Anaxarchus that the Greeks know and admire; and even if, as Celsus holds, some people ought rightly to revere a man for his virtue, it would not have been reasonable, on the strength of this, to proclaim Anaxarchus a god.

He also sends us to Epictetus, admiring what Epictetus did indeed say nobly; yet not so nobly that his saying when his leg was broken can be compared with the marvellous works of Jesus, which Celsus disbelieves, and with his words. For these were spoken with divine power, and to this day they convert not only some of the simpler folk but also many of the more intelligent.

title: The silence and gentleness of Jesus
english: And since, after his list of so many men, he says, “What did your God say that was like this, while he was being punished?”, we would say to him that by his silence under the scourges and his many torments (Matthew 27:12–14) Jesus showed more endurance and patience than any Greek who spoke out under hardship; if, that is, Celsus is willing to believe even this, recorded in good faith by men who loved the truth, who told even the marvels without falsehood and counted among them his silence under the scourges.

Moreover, when he was mocked, and dressed in the “scarlet cloak”, and the “crown of thorns” was set about his head, and he took the “reed” in his hand in place of a sceptre (Matthew 27:28–29; John 19:5), he showed the utmost gentleness, saying nothing ignoble or resentful to those who dared so much against him. It was not, then, in keeping with one who kept silent under the scourges out of endurance, and who bore with gentleness everything that his mockers brought upon him, to have said out of cowardice, as some think, the words: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39).

What seems to be a plea to be spared the cup, as it is called, has indeed its own explanation, which we have examined and set out at greater length elsewhere. But to take the saying more simply, see whether the prayer too was not spoken with piety toward God. For everyone at all regards hardship as not a matter of first choice, and yet, when the occasion calls, endures what does not come about by first choice. Moreover, the voice that says, “Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36), was not the voice of one who had given way, but of one well content with what was happening, and who put first the hardships sent by providence.

title: Abuse without proof
english: Next, I do not know why he wanted us to proclaim the Sibyl a child of God rather than Jesus, asserting that we had slipped many blasphemous things into her writings without even proving what we slipped in. He could have proved it if he had shown that the older copies were purer and did not contain what he thinks has been inserted. And without even proving that these things are blasphemous, he then again, not twice or three times but many times, called the life of Jesus “most infamous”, without stopping to deal with each of the deeds done in his life that are supposed to be most infamous; so that in saying this he seems not only to make assertions without proof, but also to revile one he does not know. For if he had set out the specific forms of a most infamous life that he saw in Jesus’ actions, we would have contended against each of the things that seemed to him most infamous.

As for Jesus having met “a most pitiable death”, the same could be said of Socrates too, and of Anaxarchus, whom he mentioned a little earlier, and of countless others. Or is the death of Jesus most pitiable, but not theirs as well? Or is theirs not most pitiable, while that of Jesus is most pitiable? You see, then, here too that Celsus’s aim was to heap abuse on Jesus. He was moved, I think, by some spirit that Jesus had overthrown and brought down, so that it no longer has the reek of sacrifices and the blood on which it fed while it deceived those who seek God in images on earth and do not look up to the One who is truly God over all.

title: Jonah and Daniel set against Jesus
english: Then, next, as if his aim were to fill up a book, he wanted us to think Jonah a god rather than Jesus, preferring Jonah, who preached repentance to one city, Nineveh (Jonah 3:4–5), to Jesus, who preached repentance to the whole world and achieved more than Jonah did. He wanted us to proclaim as a god the man who, by a prodigy and against all expectation, spent “three days and three nights” “in the belly of the sea monster” (Jonah 1:17; Matthew 12:40); but the One who undertook to die for mankind, to whom God bore witness through the prophets, Celsus would not allow to be worthy of the honour that ranks second after the God of the universe, for the mighty deeds he did in heaven and on earth. And Jonah, so as not to preach what God had commanded, was swallowed by the sea monster (Jonah 1:3, 17), whereas Jesus, because he taught what God willed, took upon himself death for mankind.

Next he says that we ought to worship Daniel, who came up from the lions (Daniel 6:23), rather than Jesus, who trampled down the savagery of every opposing power and gave us “authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). Then, having no others to name, he says, “or others still more fantastic than these”, so as to revile Jonah and Daniel at the same time; for the spirit in Celsus did not know how to speak well of the righteous.

title: Celsus says turning the other cheek came from Plato
english: After this, let us look also at his next passage, which runs as follows: “They also have a precept of this kind: not to retaliate against anyone who insults them. ‘And if he strikes one cheek,’ he says, ‘offer the other as well’ (Matthew 5:39; Luke 6:29). This too is ancient, and was said very well before them, but they have related it more crudely. For Plato too has Socrates say this in conversation with Crito: ‘Then one must in no way do wrong. – Certainly not. – Then neither must one who is wronged do wrong in return, as the many think, since one must in no way do wrong. – It seems not. – What then? Must one do harm, Crito, or not? – Surely one must not, Socrates. – What then? To do harm in return when one suffers harm, as the many say: is that just or not just? – Not at all. For doing harm to men surely differs in no way from doing wrong. – You speak the truth. – Then one must neither do wrong in return nor do harm to any man, whatever one may suffer at their hands’ (Plato, Crito 49b–c).

“These are Plato’s words, and again he says this: ‘Consider then, you too, very carefully, whether you share this view and agree with it, and let us begin our deliberation from this point: that it is never right either to do wrong, or to do wrong in return, or, when one suffers harm, to defend oneself by doing harm in return. Or do you stand apart and not share this starting point? For so it seemed to me long ago, and so it seems to me still’ (Plato, Crito 49d–e). This, then, was Plato’s view; but it had been held still earlier by divine men. But about these things, and all the others which they corrupt, let what has been said suffice; and whoever wishes to inquire further into any of them will find out.”

title: Truth is not condemned for being said plainly
english: To this, then, and to everything else that Celsus has treated as common property, saying that these things were said among the Greeks too, because he could not look their truth in the face, we must answer as follows. If a doctrine is beneficial and its intent sound, and it has been said among the Greeks by Plato or by one of the Greek sages, among the Jews by Moses or by one of the prophets, and among Christians in the recorded words of Jesus or in what was said by one of his apostles, we must not think that what is said among Jews or Christians stands condemned because the same things were said among the Greeks too; and least of all if the Jewish teachings are shown to be older than the Greek.

Nor again must we think that the same thing, said with the beauty of Greek diction, is in every way better than what is expressed more plainly and in simpler words among Jews or Christians. And yet the original wording of the Jews, which the prophets used in the books they have left us, was written in the Hebrew language and with an arrangement of words that is skilful by the standards of that language.

But if we must also show, though the claim may seem paradoxical, that the same doctrines are better expressed by the prophets of the Jews or in the words of Christians, the argument must be built from an example taken from foods and the way they are prepared. Let there be some wholesome food that gives strength to those who eat it. Suppose this food, prepared in one way and flavoured with certain seasonings, is eaten not by country people, raised on farmsteads and poor, who have not learned to eat such things, but only by the rich and those who live in luxury. And suppose that, prepared not in that way, nor as seems good to those reckoned more refined, but in the way the poor, the more rustic and the majority of men have learned to eat it, it is eaten by tens of thousands.

If, then, it were granted that from the one kind of preparation only those reckoned more refined are made healthy, while none of the many approach such foods, but that from the other the multitudes of men live in better health: which shall we approve the more, for the sake of the common good, on account of their wholesome foods? Those who prepare them usefully for the learned, or those who prepare them for the multitudes? Let it be granted that equal health and vigour come from food prepared in the one way or in the other; still it is plain that love for humankind itself, and concern for the common good, suggest that the physician who has cared for the health of the many is of more common benefit than the one who has cared for the health of a few only.

title: Divine teaching stoops to the speech of the many
english: If the example has been understood, we must carry it over to the quality of the rational food of rational beings. And consider whether Plato and the wise men of the Greeks, in the things they say well, are not like the physicians who cared only for those reckoned more refined and despised the multitude of men; while the prophets among the Jews and the disciples of Jesus, who would have nothing to do with the ornate arrangement of words, and with what Scripture has called “the wisdom of men” (1 Corinthians 2:5) and “wisdom according to the flesh” (compare 1 Corinthians 1:26; 2 Corinthians 1:12), phrases by which it hints at skill in language, might be likened to those who took care to prepare and make ready the same most wholesome quality of food in an arrangement of words that reaches the multitudes of men: one that does not sound foreign to their speech, and does not, by sounding foreign, turn them away from listening, as though such discourses were unfamiliar to them.

For indeed, if the aim of rational food, if I may call it so, is to make the one who eats it forbearing and gentle, how could the discourse that produces multitudes of forbearing and gentle people, or at least of people advancing towards these virtues, not be better prepared than the one that makes a very few, easily counted, forbearing and gentle, granting even that it does so?

And just as, if Plato, being a Greek, had wished to benefit with sound doctrines those who speak Egyptian or Syriac, he would have taken care to learn the languages of those who were to hear him, and, as the Greeks call it, to speak like a barbarian for the improvement of Egyptians and Syrians, rather than remain a Greek and be able to say nothing useful to Egyptians and Syrians; so the divine nature, which cares not only for those reckoned educated in Greek learning but also for the rest of the Greeks, came down to the plainness of the multitude of its hearers, so that, by using the words familiar to them, it might call the multitude of ordinary people to listen. Once they have been introduced, they can readily strive to grasp even the deeper of the meanings hidden in the Scriptures. For it is plain even to anyone at all who reads them that many passages can have a meaning deeper than what appears at first sight, a meaning that becomes clear to those who give themselves to examining the word, and becomes clear in proportion to the leisure they devote to the word and their zeal in its practice.

title: Jesus taught forbearance more usefully than the Crito
english: It has therefore been shown that when Jesus, speaking “more crudely”, as Celsus says, said: “To him who strikes you on the cheek offer the other also” (Luke 6:29; compare Matthew 5:39), and “to him who wishes to go to law with you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak too” (Matthew 5:40), he handled the teaching and set it before us, by speaking in this way, more usefully for life than Plato did in the Crito; for ordinary people cannot even follow Plato, and those who have learned the general studies that come before the solemn philosophy of the Greeks can do so only with difficulty.

We must also observe that the thought on forbearance is not corrupted by the plainness of the words. But in this too Celsus slanders the teaching when he says: “But about these things, and others which they corrupt, let what has been said suffice; and whoever wishes to inquire further into any of them will find out.”

title: Celsus on temples, altars and images
english: Come, let us look also at what follows, where he says this: “But let us stop there. They cannot bear the sight of temples and altars and images. Nor, for that matter, can the Scythians, nor the Nomads of Libya, nor the godless Seres, nor other nations, the most unholy and lawless. And that the Persians too hold this view, Herodotus records in these words: ‘I know that the Persians follow these customs: it is not their custom to set up images and altars and temples; rather, they even charge those who make them with folly, because, as it seems to me, they did not think, as the Greeks do, that the gods are of human nature’ (Herodotus, Histories 1.131). And indeed Heraclitus too declares something like this: ‘And they pray to these images, as if one were to chat with houses, knowing nothing of gods or heroes, who they are’ (Heraclitus, fragment 5 Diels-Kranz).

“What wiser thing, then, do they teach us than Heraclitus? He at any rate hints, in a deeply veiled way, that it is foolish to pray ‘to the images’ if one does not know ‘gods and heroes, who they are’. So much for Heraclitus; but these men openly dishonour the images. If it is because stone or wood or bronze or gold, which this man or that has made, could not be a god, their wisdom is ridiculous. For who else, unless he is a complete child, thinks these things are gods, and not offerings to the gods and images of them? But if it is because one must not even suppose them to be divine likenesses, since the form of God is different, as the Persians also think, then they do not notice that they refute themselves when they say that ‘God made man’ his own ‘image’ (Genesis 1:26–27), and his form like himself. They will agree, indeed, that these things exist in honour of certain beings, whether like them or unlike them in form; but they will say that those to whom they are dedicated are not gods but demons, and that whoever reveres God must not serve demons.”

title: The same act can spring from different doctrines
english: To this too we must say that, if the Scythians and the Nomads of Libya and the Seres, whom Celsus calls godless, and other most unholy and lawless nations, and the Persians as well, cannot bear the sight of temples and altars and images, their refusal to bear these things is not, on that account, the same as our refusal to bear them. For we must examine the doctrines that move those who cannot bear temples and images to refuse them, so that one who refuses them on the basis of sound doctrines may be praised, and one who refuses them on the basis of mistaken ones may be blamed. For the same act can come about from different doctrines.

For example, those who pursue the philosophy of Zeno of Citium shun adultery, but so do the followers of Epicurus, and so do some who are wholly unlearned. But see how great a disagreement there is among so many people about why they shun adultery. Some shun it out of regard for the common good, and because it is against nature for a rational being to corrupt a woman whom the laws have already secured to another, and to ruin another man’s household. But the followers of Epicurus, when they abstain from adultery, do not refrain for this reason; they refrain because they hold pleasure to be the end, and because many things that hinder pleasure meet the man who yields to the single pleasure of adultery: sometimes imprisonment or death, and often, before these, dangers too, in watching for the husband, and those who take his side, to go out of the house. So if, by hypothesis, a man committing adultery could escape the notice of the woman’s husband, and of all his household, and of those in whose eyes a man loses his good name through adultery, the Epicurean would even have committed adultery for the sake of pleasure.

And if the unlearned man too, at some time when he could commit adultery, does not commit it, he would sometimes be found refraining from adultery because of the fear that the law holds over him and its punishments; and it would not be in pursuit of greater pleasures that such a man abstained from adultery. You see, then, that what is thought to be one act, abstaining from adultery, is not the same but different according to the purposes of those who abstain; for it comes either from sound doctrines, or from the wicked and most impious ones held by the Epicurean, or by such an unlearned man.

title: Why Christians and Jews refuse images
english: Just as this one act, abstaining from adultery, seems to be one thing yet is found to be many, according to the different doctrines and intentions behind it, so it is with those who will not tolerate worshipping the divine at altars, temples and images. The Scythians, the nomads of Libya, the godless Seres and the Persians do this from doctrines other than those from which Christians and Jews will not tolerate what is taken to be such service of the divine. None of those peoples refuses to tolerate altars and images because he shrinks from dragging down and lowering the worship of the divine to matter shaped in this way; nor because he has come to understand that demons haunt such shapes and places, either installed there by certain sorceries or able in some other way to seize places for themselves beforehand, where, greedily partaking of the fumes of the sacrifices, they will hunt after lawless pleasure and lawless men.

Christians and Jews, by contrast, act because of the words, “You shall fear the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13), and “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Exodus 20:3; Deuteronomy 5:7), and “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth; you shall not bow down to them, nor serve them” (Exodus 20:4–5), and again, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10; Luke 4:8), and many other sayings like these. Because of them they not only turn away from temples, altars and images, but go readily even to death, when they must, so as not to defile by any such transgression the conception they hold of the God of the universe.

title: Creation is not to be worshipped
english: We have spoken earlier about the Persians, on the point that they do not build temples, yet worship the sun and the works that God has made. This is forbidden to us. We are taught not to serve “the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25), but to know that “the creation will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21), and that “the eager expectation of the creation waits for the revealing of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19), and that “the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope” (Romans 8:20). We are taught, moreover, that the things subjected to the bondage “of corruption” (Romans 8:21) and to “futility” (Romans 8:20), which do their work in a better “hope”, must not be honoured in the place of God, who needs nothing, or of his Son, the firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15). Let this suffice, then, in addition to what was said there, about the Persian nation, who turn away from altars and images but serve “the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25).

Since he also cited the saying of Heraclitus, and explained it as hinting that it is foolish to pray “to images” unless one knows “gods and heroes, who they are” (Heraclitus, fragment B5), we must say this. It is possible to know God, and his Only-begotten, and those whom God has honoured with the title “god” and who share in his divinity. These are different from all “the gods of the nations”; and as for “who they are”, they are “demons” (Psalm 96:5). But it is not possible both to know God and to pray “to images”.

title: No pretended worship and no likeness of God
english: Not only is it foolish to pray “to images”; it is foolish also to go along with the multitude and pretend to pray “to images”, as those do who follow the philosophy of the Peripatetics, and those who embrace the views of Epicurus or Democritus. For nothing counterfeit should dwell in the soul of one who is truly devout toward the divine. We do not honour images for this reason also: so that, as far as it depends on us, we may not sink into the notion that the images are other gods. That is why we also find fault with Celsus and with all who admit that these are not gods: because those who are reputed to be wise give even the outward show of honour to images. The multitude follow that show, and they not only sin, supposing that they worship the images by way of accommodation, but even sink in their souls into thinking that these are gods, and cannot bear even to hear that the things they bow down to are not gods.

Celsus, then, says that these are regarded not as gods but as the gods’ votive offerings; but he does not show how they are not men’s offerings rather than, as he named them, offerings of the gods themselves. For it is clear that these are the offerings of men who have gone astray about the divine. Nor do we suppose that the images are divine likenesses, since we do not sketch a form of the invisible and bodiless God.

Celsus supposes that we contradict ourselves when we say that the divine is not of human form and yet believe that “God made man” his own “image”, and made him in the image of God (Genesis 1:27; 9:6). To this we must say, as was said also earlier, that we hold that what is “according to the image of God” (Genesis 1:27) is preserved in the rational soul that is shaped by virtue. Here, indeed, Celsus, not seeing the difference between the image of God and what is “according to the image of God”, says that we say “God made man” his own “image” and a form like himself. But this too has been answered earlier.

title: We drive out demons and do not serve them
english: Then next he says of the Christians: “They will agree that these things exist in honour of certain beings, whether like or unlike them in form, but that those to whom they are dedicated are not gods but demons, and that whoever worships God must not serve demons.”

Yet if he had known the teaching about demons, and what each of them effects, whether summoned by those skilled in such things or giving himself of his own accord to whatever working he wishes and is able to perform, and if he had grasped the teaching about demons, which is vast and hard for human nature to comprehend, he would not have found fault with us for saying that whoever worships the God over all must not serve demons. And we are so far from serving demons that we even drive them out, by prayers and by the teachings drawn from the sacred writings, from human souls, and from the places where they have established themselves, and sometimes even from animals; for the demons often work certain things for the harm of these too.

title: Does God govern even sin?
english: In view of the many things we have said earlier about Jesus, there is no need now to repeat ourselves in answer to this: “So then they themselves are clearly convicted of worshipping not a god, nor even a demon, but a corpse.” Passing this over at once for that reason, let us look at Celsus’s next words, in which he says: “But first I will ask: why should demons not be served? Are not all things governed according to the will of God, and is not all providence from him? And whatever there is in the universe, whether the work of God, or of angels, or of other demons, or of heroes, do not all these things have a law from the greatest God? And has not whoever was deemed worthy been appointed over each thing, having received a power by lot? Shall not, then, the one who worships God rightly serve this being, who has obtained his authority from that source?” “For it is not possible,” he says, “for the same man to serve many masters” (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13).

Notice, then, how much he takes for granted even in these words, matters that need no slight examination, and knowledge as well of deeper and more secret truths about the government of the whole universe. For we must examine in what sense it is said that all things are governed according to the will of God, and whether this governing extends to sins as well, or not. If the governing extends to sins as well, not only among men but also among demons and any other being outside the body whose nature can sin, let the one who says this see how absurd it is to say that all things are governed according to the will of God. For it follows from the argument that sins too, and all that comes from wickedness, are governed according to the will of God; and this is not the same as saying that they happen while God does not prevent them. And if someone takes “being governed” in its proper sense, he is saying that the things that come from wickedness are governed (since, of course, all things are governed according to the will of God); and then no one who sins transgresses against God’s government.

The same distinction must be drawn about providence. We must say that “all providence is from him” means something true when the providence is good. But if we say, without qualification, that everything that happens is according to providence, even when something happens wickedly, then “all providence is from him” will be false; unless perhaps someone were to say that what follows as a consequence of what comes from God’s providence is also from God’s providence.

He also declares that “whatever there is in the universe, whether the work of God, or of angels, or of other demons, or of heroes, all these things have a law from the greatest God”; and what he declares is not true. For those who transgress do not transgress while following the law that comes from the greatest God. And reason shows that not only wicked men transgress, but also the wicked demons and the wicked angels.

title: Why demons must not be served
english: We are not the only ones to speak of wicked demons; nearly all who hold that demons exist do so. Not everything, then, has a law from the greatest God. For whatever has fallen away from the divine law, through its own heedlessness, vice or wickedness, or ignorance of what is good, does not have the law of God; rather, to use a new name, the one found in Scripture, it has the law “of sin” (Romans 7:23; 8:2). According to most of those who hold that demons exist, then, the wicked demons do not have the law that comes from God, but transgress it. According to us, however, all demons have fallen away from the road that leads to the good, and were not demons before; and the demons are one kind among those who have fallen away from God. Therefore whoever worships God must not serve demons.

The truth about demons is made plain also by those who summon demons for what are called love-charms or hate-charms, or to hinder undertakings, or for countless other such purposes. This is done by those who have learned through incantations and sorceries to summon demons and draw them to whatever they wish. Therefore the service of all demons is foreign to us, who worship the God over all. And the service of the reputed gods is service of demons, for “all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 96:5). This is plain also from the fact that, at the very founding of such wooden images and temples, magical rites of installation were performed in those of the so-called sanctuaries that are thought more potent; and these rites were performed by those who devote themselves to the service of demons through sorcery. For this reason we have resolved to flee from the service of demons as from destruction; and we say that all the worship of gods practised among the Greeks at altars, images and temples is service of demons.

title: Are evil spirits God’s officers or bands of robbers?
english: The words “and whoever has been deemed worthy of any task at all has been appointed over each, having been allotted power by the greatest God” also need a far deeper knowledge, one able to show which is the case. Are wicked demons appointed over certain things by the Word of God who governs the universe, in the way that executioners in cities, and those appointed over grim but necessary business in states, are appointed? Or, just as robbers in the wilderness set up one man to rule them, have the demons, as it were, formed bands in different regions of the earth and made themselves a ruler, to lead them in the deeds they have chosen, deeds aimed at stealing and plundering the souls of men?

Whoever means to speak well on these questions, so as to defend the Christians, who turn away from worshipping anything other than the God over all and His Word, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), needs also to explain the saying, “All who came before me are thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not hear them” (John 10:8), and the saying, “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy” (John 10:10), and anything else like these that is said in the sacred writings, such as, “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall ever harm you” (Luke 10:19), and, “You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 91:13).

But Celsus knew nothing at all of these things; for had he known them, he would not have said: “And whatever there is in the universe, whether the work of God or of angels or of other demons or of heroes, these things have a law from the greatest God, and whoever has been deemed worthy has been appointed over each, having been allotted power. Shall not, then, the one who worships God rightly serve this being, who has obtained his authority from that source?”

To these words he adds, “For it is not possible for the same man to serve many masters” (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13). We shall treat this in the next book, since this seventh volume, which we have written in answer to Celsus’s treatise, has now reached a sufficient length.
